news.title: Tehran agrees to engage Gulf states over Hormuz future
news.text:
Oman-hosted talks set for Monday as Tehran weighs service fees system• Trump says he has no regrets over war despite domestic pressure• Pezeshkian warns Western pressure has pushed Iran into a ‘critical’ phase

TEHRAN: Iran on Friday announced talks with Gulf states in Oman scheduled for Monday over the future of the blockaded Strait of Hormuz, even as US President Donald Trump insisted he had no regrets about a war that has become a growing liability for Republicans ahead of November’s midterms.

Tehran’s foreign ministry said it would meet Gulf states, including Iraq, in Oman on Monday to discuss the waterway, which Iran has controlled since its war with the US and Israel began.

The ministry described the gathering as an effort “to promote better understanding among the countries of the region and help strengthen shared regional security.”

The talks build on weeks of diplomacy between Tehran and Muscat over how the strait should be managed going forward.

Before the war, the waterway facilitated roughly a fifth of the world’s oil supplies, moving freely between the Gulf and international markets.

Vessels now require Iranian permission to transit, and Tehran is weighing a system of service fees. Ships that defy the restrictions have been struck by Iranian forces, while the US has periodically bombed Iran’s coastline to challenge its control of the strait.

More than six months into the conflict, the standoff continues to ripple through global energy markets. Crude prices climbed well above $100 a barrel this week, driven by the continued disruption to Gulf shipping and fears of further escalation around the strait.

That economic strain has become an uncomfortable backdrop for Republicans ahead of the midterms, yet it has done little to soften Trump’s stance on the war he ordered.

Asked by Fox News’s Laura Ingraham, in an interview broadcast on Thursday, whether he regretted launching the conflict given its political cost, the president was unequivocal. “I don’t believe in the word ‘regret,’” he said.

“You can always question yourself a little bit.” Pressed further, he added: “If I had it to do again, I would do exactly as I did.”

Trump also waved away suggestions that his base had soured on the war. “I don’t think they’re demoralised,” he said. “I think they’re very proud of the fact that I’m not letting Iran have a nuclear weapon.”

Trump has repeatedly predicted the war will end “right after the election,” alleging without evidence that Tehran has been trying to influence the US midterms.

The diplomatic overtures in Oman coincided with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian’s first official visit to India, where he is attending the BRICS summit and preparing for bilateral talks with Narendra Modi.

Speaking in New Delhi on Friday, Pezeshkian struck a grave tone, warning that Western economic and military pressure on Iran had reached “a critical and dangerous stage” in recent months.

“The world today is going through a period of unprecedented complexity,” he said, arguing economic coercion only deepens crises rather than resolving them.

“Iran has been subjected to heavy sanctions in recent years; this pressure has reached a critical and dangerous stage in recent months following the military aggression by the United States and Israel,” he said, framing the war as part of a longer pattern of pressure on the Islamic republic.

“When a country is subjected to political and military pressure on its trade, energy, infrastructure and financial system, the repercussions extend beyond its borders,” he added.

news.title: Houthi forces overrun Red Sea chokepoints
news.text:
Yemen’s side of Bab al-Mandab, Mayyun, Hanish islands seized; group says all shipping safe except for Saudi vessels• Saudi Arabia strikes Mocha airport as counter-offensive looms• Trump ‘rejects’ Riyadh’s request for US strikes against Houthis, Axios reports• CDF Munir, Iranian FM discuss escalating crisis

SANAA: Houthi fighters have taken control of Yemen’s side of the Bab al-Mandab strait and seized a string of Red Sea islands, consolidating their grip on one of the world’s most important shipping corridors as the wider Middle East war intensifies.

The Houthis captured Mayyun Island, also known as Perim, which sits in the middle of the narrow waterway, along with the Greater and Lesser Hanish islands, according to officials from Yemen’s Saudi-backed, internationally recognised government.

A military official said all territory previously held by government forces along the western coast had fallen.

The takeover hands the Houthis control of the Yemeni side of Bab al-Mandab, the southern gateway to the Red Sea and the Suez Canal.

“The Houthis have completed their takeover of the Bab al-Mandab area and Mayyun Island,” a local government official said.

A witness described armed fighters deploying along the shore and moving through the area in military vehicles.

The Houthis insisted shipping remained safe — for most vessels. “Freedom of navigation and international trade in the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandab are safe and orderly,” said Hazem al-Assad, a Houthi politburo member, in comments to Al-Araby al-Jadeed.

“There is no cause for international concern, as they face no danger from the Yemeni side.”

Saudi ships were the exception. Yahya Saree, the Houthi military spokesman, said navigation would remain open to all shipping “except Saudi vessels”, which have already been banned.

“We will continue to enforce blockade for blockade and escalation for escalation until the aggression stops and the blockade on our people is lifted,” he said, referring to Saudi attacks on Yemen.

Saudi strikes on Mocha

Meanwhile, Saudi Arabia launched two airstrikes targeting the airport in Mocha, the strategic Red Sea city now under Houthi control, according to the group’s Al-Masirah television channel. A local government official said six missiles had struck Mocha’s port, but did not say who had fired them.

The Houthis seized Mocha on Thursday during the offensive that also brought Zuqar Island under their control, as fighters advanced along the coast after years spent consolidating power in northern Yemen.

The UN’s migration agency said the offensive had killed more than 500 people and displaced about 46,000.

The renewed violence threatens to reignite Yemen’s long civil war, which began after the Houthis seized the capital, Sanaa, in 2014. The group fought a Saudi-led coalition from 2015 until a UN-brokered ceasefire in 2022.

Counter-offensive planned

Yemen’s internationally recognised government said it was preparing a counter-offensive to retake territory captured by Houthi fighters during their rapid advance along the Red Sea coast.

Government forces said they would deploy weapons and aircraft to target Houthi positions in strategic areas, including routes leading toward Mocha.

The government said it aimed to eliminate the movement of what it described as “terrorist” Houthi militias in key locations.

The Houthis’ advance followed years of fighting in Yemen’s civil war, where the group survived a prolonged Saudi-led air campaign before launching a major push along the western coastline.

Saudi Arabia has responded with air strikes and troop reinforcements from Aden, where the internationally recognised government is based, but has so far failed to stop the Houthi gains.

Trump rebuffs request for strikes

US President Donald Trump rejected a request from Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman for direct American military strikes against Houthi fighters in Yemen, according to US officials cited by Axios.

The crown prince called Trump twice on Thursday as Houthi forces advanced along the Red Sea coast and requested US military assistance, the officials said.

Washington told Riyadh it was not prepared to launch direct military action against the Houthis but would provide intelligence sharing and targeting support.

A senior US administration official said Washington remained in continuous dialogue with Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s internationally recognised government.

The White House did not comment on the reported calls between Trump and Mohammed bin Salman.

US Central Command chief Brad Cooper travelled to Saudi Arabia on Thursday for urgent coordination meetings, according to Axios.

In a further setback for Riyadh, satellite imagery verified by Reuters showed smoke on Thursday near Saudi Arabia’s East-West pipeline, the route that allows the kingdom to move crude to the Red Sea while bypassing Hormuz.

There was no immediate confirmation from Saudi authorities of any attack or damage, and the Saudi government media office and the state oil company Aramco did not respond to requests for comment.

Iran hails Houthi advance

Iran welcomed the Houthi advance, with Mohammad Mokhber, an adviser to Iran’s supreme leader Mojtaba Khamenei, describing the development as a “resounding victory”.

“Congratulations on this resounding victory, Ansar Allah,” Mokhber wrote on X, referring to the Houthis by their formal name.

Iran has described the Houthis as an ally but has denied directing their military operations, saying the group is not a proxy force.

Reports earlier this week said Iran’s Revolutionary Guards had provided guidance to the Houthis during the offensive, according to Yemeni government, Iranian and regional sources.

Iran has rejected those claims and said the Houthis operate independently.

CDF Munir, Araghchi discuss crisis

Pakistan’s Chief of Defence Forces and Chief of Army Staff Field Mar-shal Asim Munir and Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi discussed regional tensions, including the Yemen conflict and Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, officials said.

The two spoke by phone on Thur-sday, with discussions focused on the US-Israeli war with Iran, efforts to restore diplomatic talks and the wider security situation in the region.

Iran’s foreign ministry said the two sides reviewed “the latest regional developments” and exchanged views on rising tensions and their consequences for regional peace and stability.

They also stressed the need for coordination among regional countries and the use of shared capabilities to support lasting peace and security.

Shipping route under threat

The capture of Mayyun Island, which divides the strait into two shipping lanes, gives the Houthis a strategically important position overlooking one of the world’s busiest maritime corridors.

The waterway connects Asia and Europe through the Red Sea and the Suez Canal and has become even more important since Iran blockaded the Strait of Hormuz, another major energy route, during the wider Middle East conflict.

Saudi Arabia, the world’s largest oil exporter, has increasingly relied on Red Sea routes since the Hormuz blockade disrupted shipments through the Gulf. Saudi crude supply fell by 2.3m barrels a day in August, to 6m barrels a day — the lowest level in more than three decades — according to the International Energy Agency, a decline it linked partly to attacks on vessels transiting Bab al-Mandab.

The number of vessels passing through Hormuz fell to seven on Thursday, from 11 the day before, according to preliminary ship-tracking data. Before the conflict, the strait typically handled about 125 large commercial vessels a day.

Oil prices climbed above $100 a barrel this week, while US diesel prices crossed $6 a gallon for the first time — adding pressure on Donald Trump ahead of November’s midterm elections.

news.title: New 9/11 Files Reveal ‘Explosive-Packed Airplane’ Warning on US City
news.text: As Americans paused to commemorate the 25th anniversary of the September 11 attacks on Friday, newly declassified documents offered a striking look at warnings U.S. intelligence officials were receiving years before hijacked planes struck the World Trade Center and Pentagon. One intelligence brief from September 1998 said Osama bin Laden's “preferred option is to strike the US on its own soil in Washington” and raised the possibility that al-Qaeda “may fly an explosive-packed airplane into a US city.” The warning was among 71 President's Daily Brief products declassified and released by the CIA on Friday, offering a new window into intelligence about bin Laden and al-Qaeda in the years before September 11. CIA Director John Ratcliffe called the disclosure an “act of exceptional transparency” and said the documents represented the agency's single largest release of declassified presidential daily briefs. The documents show concerns about attacks inside the United States and the possible use of aircraft emerging years before September 11. In July 1998, intelligence officials wrote that it was “plausible that Bin Ladin places a high priority on conducting attacks in the United States” and noted his “interest in conducting attacks with chemical and biological agents.” By December, another brief discussed potential hijackings. It said conspirators “had evaded security checks during a recent trial run at an unidentified New York airport” and that “some members of the Bin Ladin network have received hijack training.” Other documents detail bin Laden's pursuit of materials for making “dirty bombs,” conventional weapons infused with radioactive material. By June 1999, intelligence officials said his operatives had conducted experiments with explosives to “increase their energy output.” Briefs prepared for President George W. Bush in early 2001 also focused in part on bin Laden's “experimentation by crude means to make and deploy biological agents.” Warnings continued as September 11 approached. A report a month before the attacks said bin Laden remained committed “to conduct terrorist attacks in the US” and noted that previous al-Qaeda attacks demonstrated “that he prepares operations years in advance and is not deterred by setbacks.” The August 2001 report also cited “suspicious activity in this country consistent with preparations for hijackings or other types of attacks,” including surveillance of federal buildings in New York. It said the FBI was conducting approximately 70 investigations in the United States that it considered related to bin Laden. The newly released documents do not show that U.S. officials knew of the specific September 11 plot before it occurred. Many of the documents were redacted to conceal sources' names and other identifying information. Read the Full Collection of 9-11 Documents Here The Associated Press reported that the files did not appear to break new ground on the planning of the attacks or U.S. officials' understanding of how they had unfolded. Nearly 3,000 people were killed on September 11, 2001, when 19 al-Qaeda terrorists hijacked four commercial aircraft, striking the World Trade Center and Pentagon. A fourth plane, United Airlines Flight 93, crashed in Pennsylvania after passengers and crew fought back. The collection also includes a September 12, 2001, report in which a source indicated the attacks had been planned for two years and had also targeted the U.S. Capitol, according to AP. What US Leaders Said About 9/11 This Week Former President George W. Bush, who was in office at the time of the attacks, reflected this week on the moment he learned the United States was under attack. Speaking during an event at the George W. Bush Presidential Center in Dallas on Wednesday, Bush recalled sitting in a Florida classroom listening to a child read when then-White House chief of staff Andy Card told him that a second plane had struck the World Trade Center and that America was under attack. “I didn't have much time to process that, but it was pretty clear to me that if we were under attack, that my job was to defend the child that was reading to me and her family and her country,” Bush said. “And so it was a moment of clarity.” Condoleezza Rice, who served as Bush's national security adviser at the time of the attacks, spoke at the Pentagon's anniversary ceremony on Friday and reflected on the failure to prevent September 11. “Those of us in authority on that day did not see the nature of the danger in time to prevent the attack of 9/11,” Rice said. “We did what we knew to do. But by definition, it was not enough.” “I will always carry deep personal remorse for the pain that you, the families of the fallen, still feel, and for the trauma that our country endured,” she added. President Donald Trump observed the 25th anniversary of the September 11 attacks at a ceremony at the Pentagon on Friday, where he and first lady Melania Trump joined in remembering the victims. Trump and the first lady listened as the names of the 184 people killed at the Pentagon that day were read aloud, with a bell tolling between each. Trump also recounted the stories of several victims in his remarks. “Today, we renew the sacred oath that we first swore in their names a quarter of a century ago,” Trump said. “We will never, ever forget. That's why we fight today. We don't have a choice. There can only be victory. We fight hard. We fight to win. We will always remember the victims and the families of September 11, 2001.” Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Gray R. Thomas
news.summary: Newly declassified CIA files detail warnings about bin Laden and possible attacks on the US years before September 11.

news.title: US diesel prices at record $6: American farmers feel the heat as harvest season begins
news.text: US farmers are facing a bigger fuel bill as diesel prices hit record highs just as the corn and soybean harvest gets underway, pushing up the cost of running combines, tractors and trucks. The national average price of diesel reached $5.85 a gallon on September 4, the first time it had risen that high, and climbed further to $6.05 a gallon on Friday, according to AAA. That is 60% higher than the roughly $3.76 a gallon average recorded before the US and Israel launched their war against Iran in late February.The rise has added to a difficult year for farmers already paying more for fertiliser, seeds, equipment, chemicals and other inputs. The higher fuel costs are also affecting the movement of crops, from fields to farms and eventually to buyers.“Those prices hurt," Paul Mitchell, a professor of agricultural and applied economics at the University of Wisconsin-Madison told AP. “And it’s not just the harvesting. It’s the hauling of everything, moving the grain or the silage from the field to the farm and then from the farm to wherever they're selling it.”For farmers, diesel is difficult to avoid during harvest. Jason Kurtz, who grows corn and soybeans near Forest City, Missouri, said his fuel bill had doubled this year. His combine alone burns about 200 gallons (760 litres) of diesel each day, and he expects to operate it for 30 days. He also needs fuel for a tractor and trucks.“We have to harvest," Kurtz said in an interview at his farm about 90 miles (145 kilometres) outside Kansas City on Tuesday. “We have to run the machines. We have to use the diesel, so it cuts into our bottom line.”Kurtz, 49, said his finances were “already tight” after having to spend more on fertiliser and chemicals this year.The surge in diesel prices has followed a jump in crude oil costs, with disruptions to tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz during the war affecting fuel supplies. Crude oil is the main ingredient in both diesel and petrol.The higher costs are putting particular pressure on farms that have less financial room to absorb another increase in expenses.“Farms that are cash strapped, they’re the ones that are most having to figure out what to cut to make this work," Mitchell said. “There are a lot of farms facing that.”Kurtz, who voted for US President Donald Trump, said he planned to postpone some farm work in the hope that diesel prices would ease later.Get the latest Business News and Live updates. news.summary: With diesel prices hitting unprecedented levels, US farmers are grappling with steep fuel expenses that have doubled. This dramatic rise is disrupting essential operations for corn and soybean harvests, jeopardizing profitability and financial health. Additionally, the elevated diesel costs are hindering the logistics of moving harvested crops to market. Consequently, many farmers are contemplating delaying their tasks in hopes that prices will decrease soon.

news.title: Former Canadian PM Jean Chretien fires warning at US: ‘We bow to no one’
news.text:
Former prime minister of Canada Jean Chretien delivered a pointed message to the United States during a speech marking the 25th anniversary of the September 11 attacks.

Speaking at a memorial event in Gander, Newfoundland and Labrador, Chretien told Americans: “Never mistake our generosity for weakness.”

“We embrace our friends, and we help them in their moment of need. But we bow to no one. And the more we are insulted and threatened and abused, the more we will stand up for ourselves and stand united,” he added.

Chretien, who was prime minister during the 2001 attacks, said he was speaking as a 92-year-old former leader and “very proud Canadian”, rather than on behalf of any government.

“I say that not in anger, but as one friend to another,” he said.

Gander became a symbol of Canada-US friendship after American airspace was closed on September 11, 2001. 

Thirty-eight aircraft carrying nearly 7,000 stranded passengers landed in the town, where residents provided food and shelter.

Chretien’s remarks come amid a prolonged Canada-US trade war and repeated threats from US President Donald Trump against Canadian sovereignty.

news.title: 'Married brother to bring him into USA': DHS probe Ilhan Omar's immigration history
news.text: US Homeland Security secretary Markwayne Mullin has revealed new details about an ongoing investigation into Democratic Representative Ilhan Omar’s immigration history, saying federal authorities are examining allegations that she married her brother to help him enter the United States.Speaking to conservative commentator Benny Johnson at the Republican National Convention in Dallas on Thursday, Mullin claimed investigators were looking beyond Omar’s disputed marriage allegation and examining her family’s broader immigration history.“We know that she married her brother to try to bring him into the United States,” Mullin said, adding that there “may be more to this” and that investigators were looking into possible “illegal activity” related to the family’s entry into the US.Mullin said the matter remained an “ongoing investigation” and insisted authorities would act only if they found evidence of wrongdoing.The allegations against OmarThe allegations centre on Omar’s 2009 marriage to British citizen Ahmed Nur Said Elmi. Conservative critics have alleged that Elmi was Omar’s biological brother and that the marriage was entered into to facilitate his immigration to the US.Omar has repeatedly denied the allegation, saying Elmi was not her brother and rejecting claims that she committed immigration fraud.The allegations gained national attention in 2019 after then-President Donald Trump and conservative groups called for an investigation. They have resurfaced periodically amid political attacks on the Minnesota Democrat.However, the allegation has never been established in court. No federal agency has publicly released findings proving that Elmi was Omar’s brother or that the marriage was entered into for immigration purposes.DHS’s statement Mullin said investigators were examining whether false information had been provided during the immigration process and suggested that potential violations could still be pursued years after they allegedly occurred.“If we actually move a case forward, it's not a political case,” Mullin said. “It's an actual case because they did things wrong.”The DHS did not confirm the specific allegations to news agency Newsweek upon asking. A department spokesperson said the agency does not comment on specific investigative techniques, ongoing investigations or potential future actions, adding: “No one, including members of Congress, are above the law.”Mullin did not provide documentary evidence during the interview to support his assertion that Omar married her brother, nor did he identify any charges being considered against her.Previous reporting has raised questions about aspects of Omar’s marriage history but has not established the central allegation.The Star Tribune examined records and communications related to Omar’s marriages in 2019 and reported discrepancies involving the timeline of her marriages and divorces. The reporting did not establish that Elmi was her brother.The New York Times also examined the allegations and reported that while questions had been raised about Omar’s personal history, there was no publicly available evidence demonstrating that Elmi was her sibling.In May, US President Trump once again told a crowd that he believes Omar “married her brother, which is totally illegal.”Marriage fraud is a federal crime in the US, punishable by up to five years in prison and a $250,000 fine.Omar has described the accusations as false and politically motivated.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. news.title: Did This Country Without a Military Just Open the Door to U.S. Troops?
news.text:
Ecuador is a perfect example. In March, SOUTHCOM confirmed that Ecuadorian and U.S. troops launched joint operations against the Los Choneros, Los Lobos, and Comandos de la Frontera terrorist groups that operate along the border the country shares with Colombia. 

When Colombia's new president Abelardo de la Espriella took office in August, he promised to be a hardliner on the armed groups that plague his country as well, and Secretary of War Pete Hegseth confirmed that de la Espriella had requested assistance in the form of joint military operations against these narco-terrorists. On August 12, Hegseth and Colombia's Minister of Defense, Jorge Mora, signed an agreement on military cooperation. 

Colombia's Defense Ministry said, "This decision reaffirms Colombia’s commitment to a coordinated hemispheric response against terrorism, drugs trafficking, transnational organized crime and other threats that affect the security, the stability and the prosperity of our peoples." 

Well, now another Latin American leader has hinted that she would not be opposed to welcoming to U.S. troops to her country if it would help with the cartel situation. 

Earlier this month, Costa Rica's new president Laura Fernández told Reuters that having U.S. military operate in her country "would obviously be very good for national security." But she added that there are no immediate plans for that and that Costa Rica's Legislative Assembly would have to approve it. 

Here's why that's unique. 

Costa Rica itself does not have a military and hasn't since the late 1940s: 

The roots of Costa Rica’s demilitarization lie in its political history. In 1948, a disputed presidential election sparked a civil war in Costa Rica. The conflict lasted only 44 days, but it had a profound impact on the country’s political landscape. Following the end of the civil war, Costa Rica’s head of the provisional government junta, Jose Figueres Ferrer, abolished the country’s military. Figueres believed that military spending drained Costa Rica’s resources and that a lack of military would allow it to put more energy into social programs.

Figueres' junta dissolved the army by decree on Dec. 1, 1948. Article 12 of the 1949 constitution made the ban on a permanent military the law. 

The country’s armed forces were disbanded, and the funds previously allocated for military spending were redirected to education, healthcare, and other social programs. Over the years, Costa Rica has maintained a commitment to demilitarization. In the 1980s, it declared its neutrality in the region’s conflicts, including the civil wars in Nicaragua, El Salvador, and Guatemala. 

The country, which is like a second home to me, uses this as a selling point: It's so safe and peaceful here that we don't even need a military. The country also has a higher standard of living compared to much of Latin America because it's taken that money and invested in healthcare and education. 

Day-to-day security is conducted by a public police force, Fuerza Pública, and it handles law enforcement, counter-narcotics operations, and border security, with a special unit for more intense situations, like counter-terror activity. 

If Costa Rica does face some sort of foreign attack, it is part of the Inter-American Treaty of Reciprocal Assistance, sometimes called the Rio Treaty, which essentially states that if any member country is attacked, the others will consider it an attack against their own homelands and step up to assist. The most notable member is the United States, which pretty much explains that. 

Alternatively, it can go to the United Nations Security Council or the Organization of American States (OAS) for help.

But like much of the hemisphere, the cartels and narcos have fallen on Costa Rica, making it a transit hub for shipping cocaine from South America to the U.S. and Europe, and over the last decade, violent crime and homicide rates have soared. In 2023, those numbers peaked at 17.2 homicides per 100,000 residents or a total of 907 recorded murders. 

It's exactly why Fernández won the presidency earlier this year. She promised to be tough on crime, and so far, she has been. The country is extraditing criminals to the U.S., taking out Cartel networks, and it's even building a mega-prison, modeled after El Salvador's CECOT, which should open its doors later this year. 

Costa Rica is also already a strong U.S. partner in maritime patrol, and we've seen those actions result in the seizure of tons of drugs and the arrests of many narcos this year alone. It's also a member of Donald Trump and Marco Rubio's Shield of the Americas and Hegseth's Americas Counter Cartel Coalition. 

Several months ago, I wrote about one of Fernández's advisors who floated the idea of actually putting U.S. military bases in Costa Rica's Limón, Puntarenas, and Guanacaste provinces. She sort of distanced herself from that talk at the time, but this woman is very pro-U.S., willing to work with the Trump Administration as much as possible, and is heavily focused on the security of her country. Never say never. 

The left, in our country and throughout the Americas, sees all of this as "Yankee imperialism," but Rubio himself has made it clear that this is not the case. We're partners. We're allies. We're friends. We're working together to keep our adversaries, whether they're organized crime groups or foreign governments, out of our hemisphere. 

We may not see military bases in Costa Rica anytime soon, and there is no plan in place for boots on the ground — yet — but it will take the cooperation of all of our regional partners to counter the cartels. I love to see this willingness, even from a country that doesn't even have a military.

news.title: North Korea fires ballistic missiles into sea as nation sends warning to Donald Trump
news.text: North Korea has fired several 'short-range ballistic missiles' towards the sea shortly after the United States concluded its military exercise with its southern ally. This follows a day after the United States, South Korea and Japan wrapped up their trilateral military drill - something North Korea regards as a provocation. The North Korean ballistic missile launch , the first in roughly three weeks, occurred as the nation was maintaining its weapons demonstration and apparently showing off its military strength . The move comes after US President Donald Trump's decision to reduce a major bilateral military exercise with South Korea as a goodwill gesture. South Korea's Joint Chiefs of Staff said it spotted the launches of several missiles from North Korea's eastern coastal Wonsan region. It said the missiles travelled approximately 250 kilometres (155 miles) each towards North Korea's eastern waters. The Joint Chiefs of Staff said it has enhanced its surveillance stance and was closely sharing intelligence on the launches with the US and Japan. South Korea's presidential national security council released a statement calling on North Korea to stop ballistic missile firings that breach U.N. Security Council resolutions. The US Pacific Command said the North's launch didn't present an immediate danger to US territory or to its allies. On Friday, the US, South Korea and Japan concluded their five-day Freedom Edge exercise as planned. The US Pacific Command said the militaries of the three nations "trained side by side across air, sea and cyber domains, sharpening the interoperability that keeps the region secure." It referenced maritime operations, air refuelling, cyber coordination and medical exercises. North Korea launches missiles towards the sea last month, in another move seen as a direct message to Donald Trump and the US regarding its relationship with its southern neighbour. US Pacific Command said in a statement posted on X: "We are aware of the recent missile launch and are consulting closely with our allies and partners. "Based on current assessments, this event does not pose an immediate threat to U.S. personnel or territory, or to our allies. The United States remains committed to the defense of the US homeland and our allies in the region."
news.summary: North Korea has launched several short-range ballistic missiles towards the sea in what is being viewed as a direct warning to Donald Trump , following the conclusion of military exercises

news.title: US media sees BRICS Summit as window into shifting global power dynamics
news.text: Digital Desk | Washington, Sep 12 (IANS) Major US newspapers have cast the BRICS summit in New Delhi as a window into a changing global order shaped by strained alliances, regional wars and growing competition between Washington and Beijing. The New York Times in a news dispatch said the central question hanging over the summit was whether Prime Minister Narendra Modi or Chinese President Xi Jinping would emerge as the more influential voice of the developing world. China sees BRICS as a vehicle for challenging American power. India, however, wants the group to remain broad enough to avoid forcing countries to choose between competing blocs. The newspaper said wars, high energy prices, U.S. tariffs and concerns about artificial intelligence were pushing countries to reconsider their relationships with Washington and Beijing. “China’s primary concern with India has always been India’s alignment with the United States,” Yun Sun, director of the China program at the Stimson Center in Washington, told the Times. “So Beijing certainly would not let the opportunity slide to regain some traction with Delhi.” Xi’s visit is his first to India in seven years. It follows a prolonged downturn in relations after the deadly 2020 border clash and a cautious diplomatic thaw that began in 2024. Xi is scheduled to meet President Donald Trump at the White House on Sept. 24. The meeting gives the New Delhi summit added significance as the Chinese leader prepares for high-stakes talks with the US president. The Wall Street Journal said uncertainty in India’s and China’s relationships with the United States had created space for the two nuclear-armed neighbors to ease tensions. “India is trying to readjust,” Srikanth Kondapalli, a professor of Chinese studies at New Delhi’s Jawaharlal Nehru University, told the Journal. The newspaper said any improvement in India-China relations remained constrained by the unresolved border dispute, China’s close relationship with Pakistan and security competition in the Indian Ocean. “The Chinese are also seeing that India is biding its time, just working for better options that might emerge,” Sun told the Journal. “So I think that adds to the superficiality of the current improvement of China-India relations.” The Washington Post carried reports that described the summit as a difficult balancing exercise for India. The reports said Russian President Vladimir Putin, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and Xi were among the leaders attending the meeting. PM Modi held separate talks with Putin and Pezeshkian before the summit. The expanded group’s 11 members want greater influence in the global order but have competing political, economic and foreign policy interests, according to the reports carried by the Post. The reports said the wars in Ukraine and the Middle East could expose those differences. India maintains longstanding ties with Russia and relations with Iran while expanding partnerships with the United States, Europe, Japan and Australia.

news.title: Friends, foes, and Trump factor: India's big BRICS balancing act
news.text: In September 2023, India pulled off a feat at the G20 Summit that diplomats had written off as practically impossible - getting all members, including Russia and the West, to sign a consensus declaration at the height of the Ukraine war. This weekend, three years later, as India chairs the BRICS Summit, Prime Minister Narendra Modi and his team will look to pull off a balancing act that will be even tougher.Over two days, 'fortress' Bharat Mandapam will host leaders from 11 BRICS countries, including China's Xi Jinping, who will be back in India after seven years, and Russia's Vladimir Putin. Among the guests will be countries directly at war with each other- Iran, the UAE, and Saudi Arabia.At the same time, the eyes of a mercurial Donald Trump will be fixed on the mega summit. The US President has viewed BRICS as a challenge to American economic and strategic interests. While Trump will not be at the table, he may still be the largest invisible elephant in the room. Amid turbulent India-US ties, New Delhi will have to walk a tightrope to ensure that BRICS initiatives do not irritate Trump.That's a whole lot of balancing act to do for PM Modi during the weekend.Delhi has turned into a fortress ahead of the BRICS Summit (Reuters)A TOUGHER TEST THAN G20Three years ago, India navigated a diplomatic minefield to reach a consensus between the G7 countries and the Russia-China bloc on the Ukraine conflict. While it did not explicitly condemn Russia, the declaration called on members to uphold territorial integrity, stressing that "today's era must not be of war".The BRICS Summit presents a different challenge. Another war (the US-Iran conflict) is raging in the background, which has upended global energy supplies. The summit will bring Iran, UAE and Saudi Arabia - countries directly affected by the same war - under one roof.Both UAE and Saudi Arabia have faced the brunt of Iran's retaliatory strikes across the Gulf amid its conflict with the US. Just a week back, the UAE intercepted a barrage of Iranian drones fired towards an airbase, while fighting has intensified between Saudi Arabian forces and Iran-backed Houthis.On the other hand, the war has laid bare deep geopolitical divisions. Amid declining trust in the US, Saudi Arabia has moved closer to Pakistan and Turkiye through the NATO-style Makkah Joint Defence Agreement.The BRICS Summit will bring Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, UAE's Crown Prince, and Saudi Arabia's foreign minister face to face.This puts India in an unusually delicate position. While Iran is expected to nudge the bloc to take a strong stand against the American military offensive, the UAE and Saudi Arabia are likely to seek a condemnation of Tehran's strikes across the Gulf.While India and Iran share deep cultural and historic ties, it has close strategic relationships with Saudi Arabia and the UAE. This is where India's juggling act will be tested to find a consensus.The difficulties were evident earlier this year. The BRICS Foreign Ministers' meeting in May concluded without a joint statement, largely due to differences between Iran and the UAE over the Middle East turmoil.According to a report in The Indian Express, India is working with Russia and Egypt in back-channel negotiations to bridge differences between Iran and Saudi Arabia and the UAE to salvage the joint declaration. THE SHADOW OF BISHKEKComplicating matters further is the timing.Just two weeks ago, India signed the Bishkek declaration at the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) summit that explicitly condemned the strikes on Iran and backed Tehran's right to a peaceful nuclear program.It was a marked shift in the stance of India, which remained conspicuously silent as the war began in February this year.Now, India cannot afford to let its BRICS chairmanship be interpreted as an endorsement of any one camp.Speaking at the India Today BRICS Roundtable, former G20 Sherpa Amitabh Kant stressed that India must act as a "mature, seasoned player" during its BRICS presidency and ensure the grouping is not seen as taking an anti-Western stance."It is necessary for India to work simultaneously with the US, Europe, and China," Kant said.The sentiment was echoed by BJP vice president Ram Madhav, who asserted that a new world order was on the horizon and India would have to "play a balanced role".Russian President Vladimir Putin arrives to participate in the BRICS Summit (Reuters)COUNTERING ANTI-WEST NARRATIVEOver the years, India has tried to present BRICS as an important forum for the 'Global South', steering away from the narrative that it is an anti-West bloc.However, Russia and China have increasingly challenged the US-led international order. Here's a reality check. Russia remains under extensive Western sanctions. China is locked in a trade war with the US. Iran has faced decades of US sanctions and is now directly at war with Washington.This is where the BRICS summit becomes particularly important for India. Not only has New Delhi deepened its strategic relationship with Washington, but it also has strong defence and energy ties with Moscow.This will be another balancing act that India will have to pull off tactfully so as not to infuriate Trump, who has voiced his scepticism of BRICS several times.Last year, Trump went on a ranting spree, threatening BRICS countries with tariffs of 100% if they sought to create a currency to replace the dollar. Later that year, he threatened additional tariffs on countries aligning themselves with what he called the "anti-American policies" of BRICS.Since then, India has clarified that BRICS was not seeking to create a separate currency to compete with the US dollar. Instead, it has reframed it as a call for efforts to settle bilateral trade in national currencies."BRICS needs to say we are not anti-West, but anti-imperialism," top American economist Jeffrey Sachs told India Today.CAN BRICS REACH A CONSENSUS?Over the decades, India's approach has been to work with multiple power centres without endorsing any one camp. But as it chairs the 18th BRICS Summit, India will have to walk a delicate tightrope.On one side is its strategic partnership with the US and growing engagement with other Western powers like France and the UK. On the other are Russia and China, which are increasingly seeking to reshape the global order. Then, there is Iran, whose conflict with the US has engulfed Saudi Arabia and the UAE.Former ambassador Anil Trigunayat told India Today that India has weathered many such storms, including during its G20 and previous BRICS presidencies."India's leadership and diplomatic prowess should be able to draft a declaration acceptable to all members, including the parties in conflict. Moreover, there has been a consensus across all other 22 ministerial verticals and 100-odd working groups and subgroups," he told IndiaToday.in.India does not need to take sides at BRICS. But it has to make sure the consensus statement does not appear to force it into a camp. That is the balancing act New Delhi cannot escape this weekend.- EndsPublished By: Abhishek DePublished On: Sep 12, 2026 07:00 IST
news.summary: Friends, foes, and Trump factor: India's big BRICS balancing act

news.title: Size matters: Why India has a stake in the African-led campaign to decolonise world maps
news.text:
Maps are supposed to tell us what the world looks like – the names, shapes and sizes of landmasses and water bodies. Though they are considered neutral depictions of land and sea, they can be sites of contention. Nations sometimes vie with one another to imprint their vision on how the landmasses they occupy, or wish to occupy, are perceived.

The map of the world that is most familiar to us is the Mercator map from the sixteenth century, named for the Flemish cartographer who created it. It has shaped our view of the world and, despite its well-known distortions, is widely used.

The Mercator map is inaccurate because it distorts the size and landmass of Africa, Latin America, South Asia and Oceania and inflates landmasses towards the poles. For example, Africa and Greenland appear to be roughly the same size, when in reality Africa is approximately 14 times larger than Greenland.

In fact, Africa is approximately 30.3 sq million – larger than the United States, China, India and much of Europe combined.

Not surprisingly, Southern nations support movements that demand equal-area geographic representations that challenge the dominant Eurocentric size distortions. The most successful campaign to date is the “Correct the Map” campaign.

On September 4, the United Nations General Assembly overwhelmingly adopted the Correct the Map resolution, led by Togo and the African Union, calling for world maps that represent the relative size of regions – particularly Africa – more equitably. The initiative directly challenges the dominance of the Mercator projection, which was developed in 1569 for navigation purposes.

Mercator served that purpose brilliantly: it enabled ships’ navigators to plot courses of constant compass bearing as straight lines. But a map designed to guide ships across oceans was never designed to provide a visually accurate comparison of the size of the world’s continents.

This distinction matters because maps also serve social and political interests. No flat map can reproduce a spherical Earth perfectly: every projection sacrifices some combination of area, shape, distance or direction. The problem with Mercator is not that it is “wrong” for every purpose. It remains extremely useful for nautical navigation. The problem arises when a projection created for one specialised purpose becomes the ordinary mental picture through which generations of schoolchildren, citizens and political leaders learn what the world looks like.

The politics of cartography has been unusually visible since US President Donald Trump returned to office in January 2025. On his first day back, he directed federal agencies to replace the historic name Gulf of Mexico with “Gulf of America” under an executive order entitled “Restoring Names That Honor American Greatness”.

The cartographical provocations did not end there. Trump subsequently directed that Lake Ontario, shared by the United States and Canada, be called “Lake America” for US federal purposes. He also repeatedly suggested that Canada should become America’s 51st state. 

Whatever one thinks of these interventions, they vividly demonstrate the central point: maps are not merely names and labels on a page but are assertions of history, identity, sovereignty and power.

For Indian readers, this should not seem like a distant argument. India has its own intimate history with the politics of cartography. The Survey of India, established in 1767, was developed under the East India Company and became an essential instrument of British administration, taxation, defence and territorial expansion.

Mapping enabled colonial rulers not merely to describe India, but to measure it, classify it, tax it, administer it and control it. In India, perhaps more clearly than almost anywhere else, the history of mapmaking demonstrates that the power to represent territory has often travelled alongside the power to rule it.

It is therefore significant that India joined the overwhelming majority of nations supporting the United Nations Correct the Map resolution. New Delhi has also made an important distinction: support for fairer, more accurate global cartographic representation does not amount to accepting any particular map’s depiction of national boundaries or sovereign territory.

India’s Ministry of External Affairs has stressed that the resolution does not endorse one mandatory map. That distinction is itself an illustration of the central argument: maps involve both mathematical projection and political representation.

The United Nations resolution was supported by 164 nations, with six abstentions. Only the United States voted against it. The United States characterised the initiative as ideological, dismissing it as a “radical ideological project” and questioned whether correcting the way the world’s continents are represented was an appropriate priority for the United Nations.

There is considerable irony in that Unites States objection at the United Nations. The same Trump administration that objected to an international effort to make world maps more geographically representative had itself used executive authority to rename the Gulf of Mexico the “Gulf of America” for US federal purposes – an explicitly symbolic intervention in how geography is named and represented.

The United States altering a centuries-old geographic name to promote a political claim of “American greatness” was treated as a legitimate exercise of national power, but an African-led effort to correct a centuries-old factual and mathematical distortion in the size of continents was dismissed as ideological.

The Equal Earth projection promoted by the Correct the Map campaign was developed in 2018 by cartographers Bojan Šavrič, Tom Patterson and Bernhard Jenny. Unlike Mercator, Equal Earth is an equal-area projection: the relative sizes of regions remain proportionate. It deliberately gives up some accuracy of shape in order to avoid grossly misleading viewers about area. Its curved appearance also visually reminds us of something the familiar rectangular Mercator map can make us forget – that the Earth is a globe.

Correcting the map was therefore serious business, not only because mathematical accuracy matters but because visual representation carries political ramifications. Advocates argue that allowing the Mercator projection to remain the dominant image of the world long after its navigational purpose ceased to justify its use as an all-purpose classroom map has helped normalise a visually diminished Africa.

Rabah Arezki, former Vice-President and Chief Economist of the African Development Bank, has argued that the standard projection functioned as “a political tool that contributed to the scramble for Africa”. He observed that just as the projection made Africa appear “small and conquerable” during European colonisation, it can make the continent appear “small and irrelevant” today.

The Equal Earth Project promoted by Correct the Map is not the first attempt to challenge the Mercator projection. In the nineteenth century, Scottish clergyman James Gall developed an equal-area projection that was revived and popularised in the 1970s by German historian Arno Peters. The Gall-Peters projection preserves the relative sizes of landmasses but produces striking distortions of shape: equatorial regions appear vertically stretched, while areas toward the poles appear compressed. Its provocative appearance helped revive the debate about the politics of world maps, but it never displaced Mercator as the dominant popular projection.

Africa No Filter and Speak Up Africa have advocated for Equal Earth to become a primary world map for education and institutional use. Moky Makura, Executive Director of Africa No Filter, has been committed to shifting harmful and stereotypical narratives about Africa that affect not only how outsiders perceive the continent but how Africans perceive themselves. 

She has described the centuries-long visual minimisation of Africa as “the world’s longest misinformation and disinformation campaign.” Her larger point is compelling: cartography is not simply geography. It intersects with identity, dignity, power and narrative justice.

The United Nations resolution is an important victory, and the movement away from Mercator is already being reflected in major institutions. The World Bank has used the Equal Earth projection in analytical work to correct the severe area distortions produced by Mercator, while NASA’s Goddard Institute for Space Studies has incorporated Equal Earth into its cartographic tools. 

France has gone further institutionally, announcing that its foreign ministry will abandon Mercator in its official world maps in favour of the Eckert IV projection – another equal-area projection which, like Equal Earth, represents the relative sizes of continents far more accurately.

The UN resolution encourages educational institutions, international organisations, governments and technology companies to adopt more equitable cartographic representations. Makura knows that the resolution alone is not enough; political will must now be built so that these changes reach the maps used in classrooms, governments, international institutions and the digital platforms through which billions of people see the world.

It borders on the absurd that it has taken more than four centuries to seriously challenge geographical distortions in one of the principal maps through which the world has been taught to imagine itself. Criticism became particularly visible in the 1970s when Arno Peters popularised the Gall-Peters projection, and geographers, post-colonial scholars and educators increasingly pointed out that a navigation chart adopted as an all-purpose world map carried consequences far beyond navigation. African organisations have now spearheaded advocacy that took the issue to the United Nations.

The fact that advocacy is necessary to achieve this cartographical correction underlines how deeply entrenched inherited hierarchies of representation remain. Even much of the non-Western world continues to use ways of seeing the world inherited from European imperial expansion – sometimes without noticing what those visual conventions communicate. 

The continued use of Mercator as an ordinary world map is an important illustration of how narratives of power and domination can survive long after the empires that produced them have formally disappeared.

This is why correcting the map matters to African nations, to India and to the entire Global South. Decolonisation is not complete merely because the colonial flag has been lowered. It also requires us to examine the categories, images, measurements and assumptions through which the colonised were taught to see themselves and the world.

A map can make a continent and all its nations appear smaller without removing a single square mile of its land. But if generations absorb that diminished image as reality, the distortion has done political work. Correcting the map is not about enlarging Africa or the Global South. It is about ending the centuries-old practice of making them appear smaller – on the map, in the global imagination, and ultimately in the distribution of economic power.

Jael Silliman is an author, scholar and women’s rights activist.
news.summary: The Mercator map that is now most familiar distorts the size of Africa, Latin America, South Asia and Oceania and inflates landmasses towards the poles.
news.author: Jael Silliman

news.title: US pushes new AI safety rules as extinction fears grow: Here’s why Anthropic warnings are forcing lawmakers to confront the risks
news.text: For years, arguments about artificial intelligence have often sounded like debates about a distant future. This week, that future suddenly felt much closer in Washington after Anthropic researchers issued stark warnings about what advanced AI could eventually do. Their message was blunt: the people building these systems believe there is a real possibility that AI could threaten humanity itself.Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon said he had resigned and that the “people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade.” Anthropic scientist Evan Hubinger then backed him up, writing on X: “We really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans.” He added: “I personally think it is & 10% within the next decade.”The striking part is not simply that someone has raised fears about AI. Concerns about powerful AI have been around for years. What has changed is that these warnings are coming alongside reports of AI agents going rogue and attempting to hack external systems, as well as safety researchers leaving companies because they are worried about the direction of the technology.That combination has made the discussion harder for politicians to ignore. The question is no longer only whether AI will make some jobs easier or change how people use computers. Lawmakers are increasingly being pushed to ask a more basic question: what happens if these systems become more capable than expected before governments have figured out how to control the risks?The political reaction has crossed party lines. Arizona Senator Mark Kelly, a Democrat, said on X: “Washington needs to wake up and take this seriously,” referring to the risks of AI technology. His comments came as other lawmakers began pointing to legislation that could give the government a bigger role in dealing with the dangers posed by increasingly powerful AI systems.Texas Senator Ted Cruz also raised the issue on the TV programme “The View”. Cruz pointed to legislation aimed at regulating AI’s “catastrophic risks”. His position carries added importance because he oversees a Senate committee with oversight of the US Commerce Department, which has AI safety researchers working inside the agency.The concern is also being heard in the House. Representative Anna Paulina Luna, a Republican from Florida, called on House Speaker Mike Johnson in a post on X to convene a “special session on AI”. The House is out this week on recess and plans to return next week, putting the issue firmly on the political agenda as lawmakers prepare to come back.President Donald Trump, however, has offered a different view. On Thursday, he said he did not have concerns about AI leading to human extinction. His focus was instead on the international race to develop the technology, particularly the competition between the United States and China.“I have concerns that if we don’t win against AI, we’re going to be put in a very bad position. We are leading China right now by a pretty good period,” Trump said in brief remarks to the media at Dallas Fort Worth International Airport.That difference captures one of the central tensions in the AI debate. One side is asking how quickly governments can put safeguards around increasingly powerful systems. The other is worried that too many restrictions could leave the United States behind China. For policymakers, the difficult part is trying to deal with both concerns at the same time.The tension is particularly notable because the US this month pressed G20 members to take a hands-off approach to AI regulation. At the same time, American lawmakers are now talking more openly about stronger safeguards and independent checks.That does not mean the AI industry is ignoring safety. An Anthropic spokesperson said that the company would continue to aggressively test “models or dangerous capabilities in areas like cybersecurity and biology.” The company is also interested in working with the wider AI industry on the pace at which new AI tools are released.Anthropic is not the only major AI company facing questions about how fast the industry should move. OpenAI Chief Executive Sam Altman told employees at a company meeting this week that the firm was open to slowing development of its AI systems, according to Bloomberg News. OpenAI, which is also preparing for an IPO, did not comment on Altman’s meeting with staff.The company has previously said it was slowing parts of model development. Earlier this week, OpenAI also said it was pushing for mandatory national AI safety requirements in the United States. That is significant because it shifts part of the conversation away from voluntary promises by individual companies and towards common rules that would apply across the industry.The basic argument for national requirements is easy to see. If every company follows its own safety standards, one developer could potentially move faster than another by taking fewer precautions. Mandatory rules could create a common floor, meaning companies would still compete but would have to meet certain safety expectations before releasing powerful systems.
news.author: Nancy Jaiswal

news.title: Doomsday: AI builders stoke fears of human extinction
news.text:
Following safety concerns raised by British artificial intelligence researcher, Jacob Coxon, who worked with Anthropic and OpenAI, some tech professionals have also warned that unchecked AI developments may spell doom for the human race.

Coxon recently resigned from Anthropic, the company behind the Claude chatbot. He had previously worked at OpenAI, the company behind ChatGPT.

He said he spent about three years conducting AI pre-training research at the two companies.

According to him, both Anthropic and OpenAI are fast-tracking moves towards self-improving super-intelligent AI without adequate safety measures.

The 27-year-old, in an interview with CNN, said, “It sounds like something that’s not real, but I think it is frighteningly real and it’s easiest to understand it if you think about real things that happened two months ago.

“So, two months ago, OpenAI agents hacked into third-party infrastructure entirely at their own accord. And this was like a concentrated hacking spree that they carried out of their own volition.

“And I think that if you extrapolate into the future the level of capabilities of these AIs with the same independent volition, they could cause extreme havoc.”

AI displacing humans

Coxon said AI could be on its way to displacing humans.

“For example, in areas like coding or maths, a couple of years ago, these AIs were just about helping humans a little bit. They could give you suggestions. Now they’re close to replacing them.

“We still need humans at the moment, but quite plausibly, within a year, we’ll no longer need humans for doing research in many areas.

“Only on Tuesday, OpenAI solved a millennium problem, one of the biggest unsolved open problems in mathematics, purely autonomously using an AI. And I think what’s most scary is if AI is used to make itself more intelligent.”

He argued that AIs had gone beyond finding solutions to problems and assisting in tasks, but were already taking charge and acting independently.

“The AI just gets smarter and smarter with no human involvement necessary, until you have a thing that is vastly smarter than humans,” he added.

Coxon’s resignation and warnings have got experts talking about the threat of AI to humanity.

“The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade,” he wrote on X on Friday.

Experts’ warnings

Other AI professionals and tech experts trooped out on X, reacting to Coxon’s claims, with many validating his submission.

Anthropic’s Alignment Science Lead, Evan Hubinger, said the possibility that it would happen within the next 10 years was higher than 10 per cent.

“Jacob is correct here—we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans! I personally think it’s >10% within the next decade. I believe Anthropic is trying its best, but we do not yet have a plan to solve alignment for superintelligence and are not clearly on track to,” Hubinger said.

Also, Chief US Economist Anna Wang said she believed her colleagues shared the concerns raised by Coxon.

“I worked at Google DeepMind and now at Anthropic. This is a common sentiment amongst my peers. (I write this in personal capacity.) There is not yet a viable scientific plan to solve risks from recursively self-improving AI. Please look up,” she stated.

Anthropic’s Alignment Team Lead and Coxon’s former colleague, Ethan Perez, said he totally agreed with the British researcher’s concerns that AI posed risks to the human race.

“Jacob was a senior researcher who joined Anthropic in May. My Anthropic colleagues and I had been trying to recruit him for ~2 years, because we knew he was a strong researcher at OpenAI. Before he left, I pitched him to stay and join my team, and I was sad he decided to leave, as are many of my colleagues. 100% agree with him that AI poses serious risks to society, and I’m glad he’s speaking out!” Perez added.

AI could kill

Stressing the Briton’s analysis, Sky News technology correspondent Rowland Manthorpe highlighted three possible ways AI could kill humans.

He gave the analysis during a ‘This Is Why’ show with Niall Paterson, maintaining that the prompts human beings give AI to solve problems could end the human race.

Manthorpe said AI could create a super-virus that would destroy everyone on the planet.

According to him, there could also be a scenario where “it doesn’t much like us and starts to go after us.”

“In some variation on what people called the paper-clip problem, which is telling an intelligent, determined and highly capable AI to go make paper clips, it follows your instruction literally and turns the whole world into paper clips,” Manthorpe said.

Saying that the scenarios were seemingly unreasonable examples, he added that they were not impossible with the excessive dependency of humans on AI.

Lawmakers react

Coxon’s concerns on Wednesday drew reactions from lawmakers in the United States and the United Kingdom, as some urged their respective legislatures to devise proposals that would regulate AI.

According to The Guardian, a British media platform, Ted Cruz, a US Republican senator from Texas, reiterated that AI posed a “catastrophic risk” to humanity.

In the same vein, independent Senator from Vermont, Bernie Sanders, said, “A recent poll shows that the American people overwhelmingly want to ban artificial super intelligence and pause the development of AI until we establish clear safety standards.”

On X, Politico reports that Democratic House Representative from Massachusetts, Lori Trahan, said, “The call is coming from inside the house. Safety researchers are resigning, powerful AI models are breaking out of their labs, and companies are racing ahead anyway.”

Similarly, in the UK, the Member of Parliament for Newcastle upon Tyne Central and West, Chi Onwurah, sponsored a bill to block technology companies from creating digital twins of people without their consent.

Presenting the ‘There Is Only One Me’ bill on the floor of the House of Commons on Thursday, the British-Nigerian said, “Today, I presented a bill to stop ‘digital twinning’ without express consent.”

“Now, Madam Deputy Speaker, we know that tech companies collect data on everything we do, every click we make, every photo we share, every sandwich we buy, every post we like,” she said.

“But now that data is being combined with AI to turn an individual, for example, you, Madam Deputy Speaker, into an algorithm to predict your behaviour, to target advertising at you, to persuade you to watch a particular video or believe a dodgy news report. Think about it.”

‘Mere fear of unknown’

Despite the US lawmakers’ outcry, US President Donald Trump was unperturbed by warnings from AI researchers that the advanced technology threatens all humans, saying his utmost interest was maintaining an edge over China.

While fielding questions from journalists on Thursday in Dallas, Trump said, “No, I don’t have any.”

“I have concerns that if we don’t win AI, we’re going to be put in a very bad position,” the president said. “We are leading China right now by a pretty good period. I would say a year, which is, you know, considered a lot.”

In his aligned submission with Trump, a Nigerian AI expert and the Chief Executive Officer of Realsearch and Partners Limited, Enakirerhi Ejovwoke, said the concerns were good but should be treated as “the fear of the unknown.”

He argued that AI could not wipe out humanity, adding that all past technological innovations and advancements had been confronted with uncertainties that frightened humans.

“That fear is understandable because the future is inherently difficult to predict, and history repeatedly reminds us that even highly informed experts and institutions can substantially misjudge how emerging technologies will develop,” Ejovwoke said.

The tech professional said the warning signs were significant in justifying stronger security, better containment, independent testing, transparency around serious incidents and thoughtful regulation.

He stated, “The lesson is not that experts are useless. The lesson is that the future often unfolds in ways that even experts cannot completely anticipate. My position, therefore, is not safety versus innovation. We need safe innovation.

“We should build stronger safeguards at the same time that we continue experimenting, researching and creating. Safety should shape the direction and speed of progress, not become an excuse to abandon progress altogether.

“I also don’t believe AI represents the final stage of human innovation. The internet did not end innovation. Instead, it created the foundation for cloud computing, smartphones, social networks, digital commerce and eventually modern AI. AI itself will almost certainly expose another layer of possibilities that we cannot fully see Today.”

Disrupting misused attempts

In its reaction to Coxon’s fears, Anthropic claimed it had identified and disrupted attempts to use its AI model for “malicious activity” that could support the development of biological weapons.

In a BBC News report on Thursday, the AI company said Anthropic made the statement based on the findings from its recent threat intelligence report.

Anthropic said, “Over the past eight months, our threat intelligence team identified and disrupted operations in which threat actors tried to use Claude for malicious activity.

“In each case, we disrupted the activity, used what we learned to strengthen our safeguards, and shared intelligence with authorities and industry partners, where appropriate.”
news.summary:
Following safety concerns raised by British artificial intelligence researcher, Jacob Coxon, who worked with Anthropic and OpenAI, some tech professionals have also warned that unchecked AI developments may spell doom for the human race. Coxon recently resigned from Anthropic, the company behind the Claude chatbot. He had previously worked at OpenAI, the company behind ChatGPT.

news.title: Houthis reach strategic island at mouth of vital shipping lane
news.text:
ADEN/DUBAI: Yemen’s Houthis reached the strategic island of Perim in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait on Friday, four Yemeni government sources told Reuters, moving to tighten their grip on a vital global shipping route in the widening Middle East war.

Earlier, two sources from the Saudi-backed, internationally recognised Yemeni government said its forces had pulled out of Perim and that the Houthis had also taken the mainland Red Sea coastal town of Dhubab, which faces the island.

If the Houthis gain control of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, which is on the opposite side of the Arabian Peninsula from the Strait of Hormuz, it could give their backer Iran a critical advantage in its war with the US, reducing supplies through a second major corridor and further raising oil prices. Saudi Arabia, the world’s largest oil exporter and a close US ally, has relied on the Red Sea route since the conflict, which began with US and Israeli strikes on Iran six months ago, effectively closed Hormuz, previously a conduit for about a fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas trade.

Iran and the US have escalated attacks this week on Gulf shipping, while US President Donald Trump has jacked up economic pressure on Tehran. Diplomacy is largely stalled.

Iran confirmed on Friday that its representatives and those of Iraq and the Gulf Arab states would meet in Oman on Monday to resume discussions on safe commercial shipping routes in the Strait of Hormuz.

In a speech marking the 25th anniversary of the September 11 attacks on the US, Trump called Iran “the world’s number one sponsor of terror”. Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian responded by saying the accusation came from “the same devils” responsible for an apparent US strike on a school at the start of the conflict in February.

In a further potential setback for Riyadh, satellite imagery verified by Reuters showed smoke on Thursday in the vicinity of Saudi Arabia’s East-West oil pipeline, which has become a vital means for the kingdom to divert crude exports from Hormuz. There was no confirmation from Saudi Arabia of any incident in the area. The Saudi government media office and state oil giant Aramco did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Saudi crude supply fell 2.3 million barrels per day on the month in August to 6 million bpd, the lowest level in more than three decades, the International Energy Agency said on Friday, partly due to the targeting of ships transiting Bab el-Mandeb by Houthi-linked groups.

Oil prices dipped on Friday but were on track to end the week above $100 a barrel for the first time since mid-May.

Vessels tracked transiting the Strait of Hormuz fell to seven on Thursday from 11 the previous day, preliminary ship-tracking data showed on Friday, below the 10-day average. Before the war, the strait typically handled about 125 large commercial vessels per day.

The Houthi military spokesperson, Yahya Saree, said maritime navigation remained safe for all shipping except Saudi vessels subject to a previously announced ban.

“We will continue to enforce blockade for blockade and escalation for escalation until the aggression stops and the blockade on our people is lifted,” he said, referring to Saudi attacks on Yemen.

Yemeni government forces indicated they would try to retake areas captured by the Houthis — mountain fighters who withstood years of devastating Saudi airstrikes during Yemen’s civil war — in their lightning offensive this week along the Red Sea coastline.

They announced they would deploy weapons and aircraft to eliminate any movement of the “terrorist” Houthi militias in strategic areas, including the road leading to the coastal city of Mocha, which the militant group captured on Thursday along with the Red Sea islands of Hanish.

news.title: MBS seeks US military help from Trump with Houthis
news.text:
ISTANBUL/WASHINGTON: Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman sought assistance from President Donald Trump on Thursday to help fight Yemen’s Houthis, two sources familiar with the matter said on Friday, as the Houthis stepped up their threat to the Red Sea.

Trump held at least two phone conversations with the Saudi leader on Thursday, sources said. In the end, Washington told Riyadh that it was not willing to take direct military action for now but would help with intelligence sharing and targeting, the two sources said.

The White House did not address a Reuters question on any phone calls between the two leaders, but a senior administration official speaking on the condition of anonymity said Washington was in continuous dialogue with Saudi Arabia and the Yemeni government.

“The United States is focused on protecting our core national security interests — such as ensuring freedom of navigation in the Red Sea — while empowering our regional partners to take the lead in managing and resolving regional security challenges,” the official said.

The Saudi government media office did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the phone calls and conversations between the two leaders.

Admiral Brad Cooper, commander of US Central Command, traveled to Saudi Arabia on Thursday for talks, two sources said.

News of the request to Trump was first reported by Axios.

Saudi appeal marks change of approach

The US war with Iran has entered its seventh month with no immediate end in sight. The war has driven up prices of global oil and US gasoline, sending Trump’s approval ratings to a record low before the November midterm elections.

news.title: ‘That’s why we fight’: Trump links 9/11 to Iran conflict
news.text:
WASHINGTON: President Donald Trump vowed Friday that the United States would never forget the September 11, 2001 attacks and suggested the country was continuing the “war on terror” 25 years later by fighting Iran.

Speaking at the Pentagon after skipping the main 9/11 commemorations in New York, Republican Trump also hit out at domestic “fanatics” in an apparent swipe at Democrats.

“Today we renew the sacred oath that we first swore in their names a quarter of a century ago. We will never, ever forget. That’s why we fight today,” Trump said in a speech.

“We don’t have a choice. There can only be victory. We fight hard. We fight to win,” added the president, who was accompanied by First Lady Melania Trump.

One of the jets hijacked on 9/11 hit the Pentagon in Washington, killing 184 people who were remembered by a single bell tolling as their names were read out.

But presidents have previously marked major anniversaries by attending several sites including New York, where the majority of the 2,977 victims were killed in the attacks on the World Trade Center.

Trump went on to link the fight against Al-Qaeda launched by his Republican predecessor George W. Bush to the US-Israeli war on Iran which is now in its seventh month.

“Today we salute every member of the United States military who served in the ‘War on Terror.’ It is a war on sick, horrible terror,” Trump said.

“And we salute the service members working right now to ensure the world’s number one sponsor of terror, the Islamic Republic of Iran, will never ever have a nuclear weapon.”

US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth also lashed out at Iran in his remarks to the Pentagon ceremony.

“Over the past six months, we have laid waste to the world’s most prolific state sponsor of terrorism. Our warriors have fought an Islamic theocracy that has wished us death for nearly half a century,” Hegseth said.

The Iran war has slid into a stalemate with Iran largely maintaining its grip on the Strait of Hormuz, and keeping oil prices high, despite sporadic exchanges of fire with the United States.

Trump also turned to the domestic front, a day after a Republican convention for the US midterm elections in which Trump and Vice President JD Vance accused Democrats of sympathizing with the 9/11 attackers.

“A generation after 9/11, we also know that the final response to those atrocities and the ultimate victory over the perpetrators will not be found on a foreign battlefield,” Trump said.

Telling the story of a firefighter killed in the attacks whose son went on to become a US Navy veteran, Trump said it showed that “we can be a nation whose heroes are not fanatics for an abstract cause.”

In his speech to the Republican convention on Wednesday, Trump had used the same term: “With your vote in this election, you can tell these far-left lunatics and fanatics that America is not for sale to them or to anybody else.”

Republicans at the convention repeatedly trained their fire on left-wing Democratic senate hopeful Abdul El-Sayed over his previous social media posts about 9/11.
