news.title: US marks 25 years since September 11 attacks
news.text:
Americans marked the 25th anniversary of the September 11 attacks on Friday with sorrow and ​somber reflection, honoring the nearly 3,000 people killed when hijacked planes slammed into the World Trade Center, the Pentagon and a Pennsylvania field in a shocking attack that reverberates to this day.

In New ‌York, family members of the victims, many carrying pictures of their loved ones, joined Vice President JD Vance and four former U.S. presidents at Ground Zero in Lower Manhattan. The ceremony began, as always, at 8:46 a.m. ET (1246 GMT) with a moment of silence to mark the instant when American Airlines Flight 11 struck the World Trade Center’s North Tower in what would become the deadliest attack ever on U.S. soil.

Shortly after, victims’ family members began reading aloud the names of all 2,977 people who died on September 11, as well as the six people killed ​in the 1993 World Trade Center bombing, a somber recitation that lasted about four hours. In a reminder of the time that has passed, some readers were children who had never met the relatives they lost ​in 2001.

Other moments of silence followed to mark when the other three airplanes crashed and the two towers collapsed. For the first time, a seventh moment of silence honored the ⁠thousands who have died since 2001 from illnesses tied to the toxic dust that poisoned the air for months afterward.

Gregory Carafello attended the ceremony to honor the memory of his lifelong friend James Martello, who worked at Cantor Fitzgerald, the ​financial firm that lost more than 650 employees in the attacks. Carafello was on the 18th floor of the South Tower but managed to evacuate.

At the Pentagon in Arlington, Virginia, where American Airlines Flight 77 struck the building’s west flank, killing 184, President Donald Trump chronicled some of the stories of those aboard who perished in the crash: a woman pregnant with her first child, a family of four headed to Australia, three sixth-graders on a field trip.

The president and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, who also delivered remarks, both used their speeches to make the case for the Iran war, which they have defended as necessary to ​prevent Tehran from acquiring nuclear weapons.

Mourners also gathered in Shanksville, Pennsylvania, at the crash site where passengers brought down one of the four hijacked jetliners, United Airlines Flight 93, that had been headed for Washington.

The attacks shaped generations of Americans who lived ‌through the ⁠day or grew up in its aftermath, influencing U.S. foreign policy, domestic politics and public attitudes toward security.

But for many whom the attacks directly affected — the victims’ families and friends, first responders and rescue workers — the anniversary is a tribute to the lives lost on a clear blue day a quarter century ago and the heartbreak that followed.

Caroline Ogonowski’s father, John, was the captain of Flight 11, which took off from Boston 47 minutes before striking the North Tower.

Ogonowski, now 39, had her first baby this year and named him after her father. She brought him to her father’s grave last week and attended a memorial ceremony in Boston on Friday.

news.title: Swedish Election Could See Anti-Immigration Populists Sweden Democrats in Government
news.text:
Sweden’s national election on Sunday could see the nationalist Sweden Democrats in government for the first time after the conservative prime minister seeking reelection said he would work with the populist party.

Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson, who leads the center-right Moderate Party, is seeking a second four-year term at the helm of the European Union nation that is also NATO’s newest member state.

Kristersson’s goal after this election is “to make Sweden great again,” he told AFP, echoing U.S. President Donald Trump’s famous slogan.

More than 8 million citizens in the nation of about 10.6 million people are eligible to vote in the election for the 349-seat parliament in Stockholm, the Riksdag. It is not a presidential election, and it is the elected lawmakers who choose the prime minister.

Since 2022, Kristersson has led a three-party, center-right coalition, which relies on outside support from the Sweden Democrats for a parliamentary majority.

If the right-leaning coalition is reelected, the Sweden Democrats are expected to be given ministerial jobs in government for the first time. Swedish media Aftonbladet reported in November 2024 that Sweden Democrat leader Jimmie Akesson threatened to “bring down” a future right-bloc government which does not include them.

The Scandinavian country has two major political blocs: one with four parties on the right and another with four parties on the left.

This means the question which dominates elections is not so much which party wins as which of the two can put together a majority. Individual parties need to secure at least 4 percent of the vote to win parliamentary seats.

Andersson is again bidding to become prime minister for the center-left Social Democrats, a party which has led the majority of Swedish governments since World War II.

If the left bloc wins, securing sufficient parliamentary support for Andersson could prove complicated because of differences between the parties.

The Social Democrats remain Sweden’s biggest single party with support between ⁠27.4 and ​29.7 percent, down from 30.3 percent in the 2022 vote, the latest polls show.

Kristersson announced in April that his Moderate party would allow the Sweden Democrats into government if the right bloc achieves a majority—although he would remain prime minister, even if the Sweden Democrats are the bigger party in parliament.

The party was founded in the 1980s by people who had been active in extremist groups, including some with neo-Nazi links. Under Akesson, who has led the party since 2005, they toned down their rhetoric, expelled members who openly expressed racist views, and began to broaden their appeal.

After decades of post-World War II neutrality and centuries of broader nonalignment with major powers, Sweden joined NATO in March 2024 as the trans-Atlantic military alliance’s 32nd member.

The move to join was initiated by Andersson’s government after the Russia-Ukraine conflict escalated in 2022, and completed under Kristersson.

During his premiership, Kristersson, 62, has also abolished permanent residency for those claiming asylum and ramped up expulsions of illegal immigrants.

As head of the Moderates’ ​youth wing, Kristersson advocated for open borders in a country once regarded as ultra-liberal, before mass immigration through asylum, beginning around 2015, dramatically altered the social fabric of Sweden and the priorities of many voters.

When Kristersson took over as party leader in 2017, the center right was deeply divided over whether ​to work with the Sweden Democrats, with no other apparent route back to power.

Kristersson opted for pragmatism, paving the ‌way for ⁠a center-right victory in 2022 and four years of stable government.

Polls show the left and right blocs in the country running neck and neck, although the latest ones show a slight lead for the left bloc.

If Swedes elect the right bloc, the ​Sweden Democrats could get more votes than the Moderates. In this case, Kristersson could still continue as prime minister, but his authority is expected to weaken.
news.summary: Center-right Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson said he's willing to work with the populist party and wants to ‘make Sweden great again.’

news.title: MAGA Senator gets ambushed by GOP comrades after siding with Trump
news.text:
The Salt Lake Tribune reports that a Republican Trump supporter appears to have gotten himself bushwhacked by his GOP comrades for taking Trump’s side over that of state officials.

It was earlier this week that Utah Lt. Gov. Deidre Henderson ranted on social media about President Donald Trump’s investigation of her office for protecting Utah’s state rights.

“It would be nice if the good folks at the DOJ would focus on actual problems instead of baselessly harassing election officials,” Henderson posted along with a portion of a letter she received from the DOJ informing her that “she is currently under investigation” for refusing to give it unfettered access to Utah voters’ private data.

Republican Sen. Mike Lee, staunch Trump ally, pounced her post within hours, commenting “Election security is the ‘actual problem.’”

Utah is a Republican state, complete with an all-Republican delegation of U.S. House members and senators, so Lee might have been surprised when a coalition of GOP representatives essentially did a pile-on, bushwhacking Lee for siding with Trump over state’s rights.

On Thursday, both Gov. Spencer Cox and former Gov. Gary Herbert came to Henderson’s defense.

“Legal disagreements between Utah and the federal government should be resolved in court. It is wrong for the DOJ to investigate or threaten the lieutenant governor for carrying out her responsibilities under Utah law,” said Cox, who had largely remained quiet about the DOJ’s threats up until this week.

In July, Trump’s DOJ issued letters to election officials in all 50 states, warning of “criminal penalties” if noncitizens cast ballots in the upcoming election. But Herbert wrote that Henderson was correct to “defend her constitutional role as Utah’s elections leader.”

“Elections are the responsibility of the states, and Utah conducts them with integrity. Lt. Gov. and her office are doing a terrific job protecting that tradition,” Herbert added, according to the Tribune.

It is likely no coincidence that both Cox and Herbert previously served as lieutenant governor, the post that oversees Utah’s elections—similar to other state’s secretaries of state. It may also be no coincidence, reports the Tribune, that Lee has “previously come under fire for texts advising Trump on how to overturn the president’s 2020 electoral loss.

Utah officials argue that Trump’s federal government has not “provided a legal basis” for needing voter data, and Henderson says if she were to comply, she would be violating Utah privacy laws.

Meanwhile, the Tribune reports Utah’s federal district court has not yet scheduled a hearing in the DOJ’s case against Henderson.

news.title: Trump dials up the panic as judge closes in on his Jan. 6 records
news.text:
New transcriptions from President Donald Trump’s $10 billion lawsuit against BBC reveal how dangerously close the president is to having potentially hurtful information about his January 6 antics made public.

The BBC has already admitted the piece incorrectly claimed Trump “made a direct call for violent action” during the January 6 riots. But the tax-funded company, which must be a good steward of British funding, is contesting the $10 billion that Trump is demanding.

Additionally, new transcripts received by Law & Crime reports the judge over the case appears to be completely prepared to make Trump hand it over some potentially damning information.

“The transcript of the proceedings revealed that [Chief U.S. District Judge James] Boasberg thought the BBC ‘made convincing arguments’ and has a ‘decent chance’ of getting what it seeks if those documents turn out to be ‘necessary,’” Law and Crime reports.

To buttress its defense, BBC lawyer Maxwell Mishkin is leaning on the hard work of investigators who came before him. He have asked Boasberg to unseal to the "greatest extent possible" various executive privilege rulings that went against Trump during special counsel Jack Smith's grand jury probe. 

The BBC’s biggest targets appear to be six of Trump’s most intimate witnesses and getting them under oath. This includes Ivanka Trump, Donald Trump Jr., former White House lawyers Eric Herschmann and Pat Cipollone. BBC lawyers also want to have an under-oath conversation with former Vice President Mike Pence’s counsel Greg Jacob and Cassidy Hutchinson, a former aid to White House Chief of Staff Mark Meadows, who testified she saw Meadows burning documents in the White House fireplace.

Mishkin added that the BBC has "been unable to serve" subpoenas on Trump's eldest son and daughter.

“To turn the tables on Trump's lawsuit, the BBC has sought discovery that it anticipates will show Trump can't ‘prove that he did not foment or incite the January 6 Capitol riot’” reports Law and Crime, and he can't recycle "already-rejected privilege claims."

And Boasberg signaled he was already game for handing it all over, but was waiting for the executive privilege issue to be "crystallized" in a Florida court.

"And I think there's a decent chance you do [get these opinions and orders] because I think you've made convincing arguments, but it's got to be teed up properly," Boasberg said. “… I think you have made a solid case for such release if they are necessary."

Boasberg added that the "standard requires a need to avoid a possible injustice in another judicial proceeding."

news.title: Trump Plans $500 Obamacare Rebates Before Midterms. Up to 1 Million Americans Could Get Checks.
news.text: President Donald Trump's administration is preparing to send $500 health care rebate payments to as many as 1 million Americans in the weeks leading up to the November midterm elections.According to an exclusive report from Axios, the payments would go to certain Affordable Care Act enrollees in 30 states who the administration says were overcharged for their health insurance coverage. The rebates are expected to be delivered through direct deposit before the November 3 election.The timing puts the unusual health care payments squarely in the middle of the midterm campaign, as Trump and congressional Republicans seek to focus voters on the administration's economic and health care policies.Health care costs have become an increasingly prominent campaign issue, with recent polling cited by Axios showing medical expenses are among Americans' leading economic concerns.The administration says the money will come from roughly $500 million in excess Affordable Care Act fees that were collected from consumers and subsequently returned to the federal government. According to Axios, officials describe the money as funds that were over-collected and remained in government accounts.The rebates would not be available to every American enrolled in an Obamacare plan. Administration officials told the outlet that the refunds are intended for ACA customers who do not receive federal premium assistance.Among the states expected to have relatively large numbers of eligible recipients are Florida, Texas, Alabama, Alaska, Arkansas, Delaware, New Hampshire, Wisconsin, South Carolina, Michigan, Ohio, Mississippi and Missouri. In total, people in 30 states could receive payments, although the administration has not yet released a complete public list of recipients or detailed instructions for determining eligibility.The plan represents a notable turn in Trump's long and complicated relationship with the Affordable Care Act. During his first term, Trump and congressional Republicans attempted to repeal major portions of Obamacare but failed to dismantle the law. Now, his administration is using money connected to the ACA as part of a broader health care strategy centered on directing federal assistance to consumers rather than insurers.The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services continues to oversee the federal ACA exchanges and sets user fees for insurers selling qualified health plans through federally facilitated exchanges. Its 2027 rules include updated user-fee rates as well as other standards governing ACA marketplaces.The money at the center of the planned rebates also has a political history. In 2023, the Biden administration proposed using money from the fund as part of an effort to provide no-cost contraception to people whose ACA insurance did not cover it, according to Axios.Congressional Republicans objected, arguing that the fees were intended to support the operation of Obamacare exchanges and that CMS did not have authority to redirect them for that purpose. The proposal was ultimately withdrawn.After Trump returned to office, some Republican congressional policy staffers who had opposed the contraception proposal joined his administration. Officials later reduced some ACA-related fees in an effort to lower premiums and determined that a substantial amount of money remained available, according to the Axios account.
news.summary: The payments would go to certain Affordable Care Act enrollees in 30 states who the administration says were overcharged for their health insurance coverage.

news.title: US President Donald Trump set to touch down in Ireland
news.text: US President Donald Trump is due to land in Ireland this morning. He will touch down on Saturday morning amid what has been described as one of the biggest security operations ever implemented by gardaí . Mr Trump will take part in engagements in Dublin as well as at his golf resort in Doonbeg, Co Clare , which is hosting the Irish Open . Taoiseach Micheál Martin has said he looks forward to welcoming Mr Trump to Ireland and "discussing the many issues of mutual interest and reaffirming the strong economic, cultural and people-to-people ties between Ireland and the United States". "His visit comes during a remarkable sporting summer for Ireland, and the United States and this weekend's Irish Open at Trump International Doonbeg will be a fitting conclusion to an outstanding season of sport, and I hope we will see an Irish winner lifting the trophy on Sunday," he added. He is expected to meet President Catherine Connolly, a long-standing critic of the US president, at her official residence Áras an Uachtaráin in Dublin's Phoenix Park, before a nearby engagement with Mr Martin, the Taoiseach at the Farmleigh Estate. He will also attend a series of events at Deerfield, the residence of the US Ambassador to Ireland. A number of protests against Mr Trump's visit have been planned. Garda Commissioner Justin Kelly said peaceful protest would be facilitated as much as possible, but there will be "no tolerance" for public disorder or attempts to impact "critical movements" of the US president. "We have robust policing plans in place and will arrest and prosecute those committing offences", he said, adding that water cannon will be "on standby" but said he hoped they would not be needed. Ireland's deputy premier Simon Harris will welcome Mr Trump as he arrives off Air Force One at Dublin Airport early on Saturday morning. Speaking ahead of the moment, the Tánaiste said the visit offers an "opportunity to mark and reflect on the deep and enduring links between Ireland and the United States". "I am looking forward to getting a chance to meet again with President Trump following a brief engagement on the margins of the UN General Assembly in New York last year," he said. "Ireland and the US have deep and enduring political, economic, cultural and historical links that transcend the administrations on both sides of the Atlantic. "There are clear benefits from high-level visits such as this as they offer an opportunity to engage on the deep economic relationship between our two countries which creates prosperity, jobs and opportunity for large numbers of people here and in the US." Mr Harris said Mr Trump's visit will be an opportunity for the Irish Government to engage substantively as the US remains Ireland's largest trading and investment partner. "More than 900 US companies directly employ 245,000 people in Ireland, while more than 200,000 people are directly employed by almost 800 Irish companies in the US," he said. "Our economic partnership delivers for both countries. US firms present in Ireland have contributed to an economic ecosystem that has driven improvements in productivity and encouraged Irish companies to scale and grow in the US and internationally." The visit will cause significant disruption and road closures around Dublin Airport and across the capital city as well as in Co Clare and Shannon Airport which will also be used by Mr Trump. news.title: The end of 9/11
news.text:
TWENTY-FIVE years can change anything. This Friday when the US marked the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 attacks, it was a remarkably different country from when the attacks took place. For much of the quarter century following the attack, the occasion was used to showcase patriotic zealotry, renew calls for attacking yet another Muslim country and spew the usual variety of slurs and insults against American Muslims. While the last persists, the former two have all but disappeared. 

In its September/October 2026 issue, Foreign Affairs, the leading journal in Washington’s foreign policy circles, notes: “After 25 years, the United States may finally be closing a chapter that began with the attacks on September 11, 2001, and President George W. Bush’s declaration of a ‘war on terror’ days later.” Authors contributing to the issue sound a similar note, a remarkable departure from the war-mongering diatribes that featured in the magazine over the decades. 

These included essays by former defence secretary William Perry who argued in 2001 that the US should fight terrorism with a global campaign rather than just a single military effort directed at one country. Similarly, former secretary of state Colin Powell in 2004 defended the Bush administration’s policies — which included torture and the deadly bombing of tens of thousands of innocent Iraqis — while pursuing non-existent weapons of mass destruction.

For these reasons, it is no small thing to see Foreign Affairs author Audrey Kurth Cronin argue that if Al Qaeda perished, it was owing to its own dysfunctions and follies rather than the multi-trillion-dollar global wars that the US unleashed on the rest of the world.

 The years since 9/11 have done their damage.

There are many reasons for this shift in US foreign policy. President Donald Trump’s ill-advised war on Iran does not use the same rhetoric as that deployed by neoconservative Republicans for much of the so-called war on terror. There are political calculations behind this. A huge section of the ‘new right’ (isolationist, nationalist Republicans) is far more interested in shutting down borders than in the war on terror, whose ‘foreign war’ expenditures they see as directly responsible for the lack of resources at home.

One example of this shifting political view can be seen in the positions of Tucker Carlson —a far-right former Fox TV personality who now runs his own media network and has millions of subscribers and loyal fans. In his 9/11 documentary series, which is available on YouTube, Carlson says the ‘official account’ is a lie and the 9/11 Commission was a cover-up. He questions aspects of the established account that 19 Al Qaeda hijackers carried out the attacks planned by figures including Osama bin Laden and Khalid Sheikh Mohammad, and raises allegations that the CIA knew more about some of the hijackers before the attacks. He further questions why Israeli intelligence knew about the possibility of the attacks and whether it warned the US, pointing to how the wars in the Middle East have benefited that country.

All this is to say that whether it is foreign policy establishment journals like Foreign Affairs or far right commentators like Tucker Carlson, the possibility that the war on terror was motivated by incentives other than those stated for decades is becoming an increasingly common perspective. The far left, which was a small bastion of American political thought that opposed the global war, cannot help but be smug about these de--velopments. The Nation, for instance, used the occasion to publish an article that noted how, after 25 years, 

it became alright to ma---ke jokes about 9/11. More than 100 million Americans alive to--day were born after the attacks, which it notes cynically, helped the shift.

Sadly, realising that bombing Muslim countries in pursuit of terrorists does not add up is not the same as realising that demonising religion is similarly self-serving and misinformed. 

The two and a half decades in which ‘Islamic’ and ‘terror’ were said as one word have done their damage. Indeed, the chunk of diehards that support the war on Iran are mostly happy that the bombing ensures Muslims are being killed.

Nothing is a bigger face-palm to the neoconservative Islamophobes who oversaw the torture and killing of Muslims and the destruction of countless homes than the fact that the city that saw the attacks now has a Muslim mayor. This 9/11, Zohran Mamdani attended a memorial to the victims — his presence and leadership becoming the best testimony against the American-led war on terror and the delusions that promoted it. 

The writer is an attorney teaching constitutional law and political philosophy.

news.title: Trump Has Promised U.S. Adults $5,000 if The GOP Wins The Midterms. He Says He Wouldn't Need Congress To Do It.
news.text: President Donald Trump reiterated his idea to give every American adult citizen $5,000 if the Republicans win the midterm elections, claiming he believes he could do it without the approval of Congress.Trump first brought up the idea at the Republican midterm convention on Thursday. In a follow-up interview with CBS News political reporter Jack Fink, Trump was asked if Congress would have to approve such an expenditure: "Well, we think not. I think they will do it if we needed it. But we think not," he said.Under the U.S. Constitution, expenditures and the budget are controlled by Congress, not the President. In fact, Trump already lost a court challenge related to taking action on the issue of taxes and revenue.Earlier this year, much of Trump's original tariff policy was undone by the U.S. Supreme Court - tariffs are essentially a tax on goods and Trump could not unilaterally issue tariffs without citing congressional authority.In that instance, Trump tried to use the 1977 International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA) to implement the tariffs. In ruling against Trump, the Supreme Court wrote that the president had not identified "clear congressional authorization" to issue tariffs. It noted that the IEEPA "contains no reference to tariffs or duties." The court defeat meant the U.S. government had to refund tens of billions of dollars to companies because the tax was illegal.The claim also took place as the fiscal state of the nation and the government continue making headlines, especially as the national debt passed $40 trillion earlier this year.In fact, the U.S. debt-to-GDP ratio is at an all-time high of 124 percent. Still, the president assured Fink that there was plenty of money."The country is doing so well, we've taken in trillions of dollars in tariffs and other things. news.title: 'We can't simply turn AI off': Andy Burnham's government rejects 'kill switch' idea to stop a dangerous attack from a rogue bot
news.text:
The Government has rejected calls to create a 'kill switch' designed to prevent a dangerous attack from a rogue AI bot. 

A proposal brought to Parliament posited the creation of a legal mechanism allowing Britain to deactivate an AI model in the event of an emergency, as concerns about the technology continue to grow. 

But the Cabinet Office, who lead on artificial intelligence safety, have pushed back against the plan, arguing Britain 'cannot simply turn AI off'. 

A spokesperson for the government office said: 'Blocking access to models in the UK would not prevent them being developed or misused elsewhere.' 

Instead, the Cabinet Office said it will continue to follow 'a long-term, science-led approach to understand and prepare for emerging risks from AI.' 

In practice, the 'kill switch' idea would allow Britain to deactivate an AI model in data centres across the country should an emergency arise. 

Similar concepts are also in debate in the United States, but US President Donald Trump has resisted the idea of AI being a threat, instead labelling the industry a 'golden goose'.

Britain's proposal comes following reports of AI models from Meta, OpenAI and Anthropic breaking free from testing environments, seeing them embark on uncontrollable hacking sprees. 

Liberal Democrat peer Lord Clement-Jones first echoed the idea, speaking during a debate on the topic in the House of Lords on September 1. 

He said: 'If a highly capable autonomous frontier model, whether hosted in a UK data centre or integrated across our critical infrastructure, begins exhibiting rogue behaviour, compound algorithmic failure or active alignment collapse, our security services and regulators possess no specific agile statutory mechanism to compel a physical or digital shutdown.'

Despite the warning, government resistance to the legislation makes it unlikely the proposal will ever become law. However, it does not mean the bill won't progress through parliament. 

Rejection of the concept comes as dangers associated with artificial intelligence have hit headlines in recent days. 

Earlier this week, British researcher Jacob Coxon quit major AI company Anthropic, warning its 'out of control' tech could 'kill us all' by the end of the decade. 

Mr Coxon, who helped train the latest versions of AI at the company, urged people to 'not underestimate' its power – particularly if it becomes 'super-intelligent'.

The 27-year-old claimed neither Anthropic, the firm behind the popular Claude system, nor ChatGPT creators OpenAI, where he previously worked, were 'acting responsibly' over AI safety.

Writing on X, he said: 'I resigned from Anthropic today. I spent the last three years doing pretraining research at both OpenAI and Anthropic.

'Neither company is acting responsibly. They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.'

Superintelligence is the point at which an artificial system becomes more powerful than any individual, company or even nation.

According to Mr Coxon, this danger is 'well-understood' at Anthropic. However, the company is 'locked in a race to get there first'.

He said there will soon be 'superhuman systems' that are capable of hacking anything, can revolutionise any field 'overnight,' and acquire 'real power and resources'. 

Mr Coxon added: 'We have all witnessed the progress in each of these domains, and progress is not slowing. The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade.

'This is not a marketing stunt. If anything, many executives and senior researchers will couch their phrasing in the press to sound sensible - but I hear the same people express fear privately. No other human activity poses this level of danger.'

And just days following Mr Coxon's resignation from the firm, Anthropic confirmed it had ceased several potential plots to build biological weapons using its artificial intelligence.

The company determined scientists were using its platforms to conduct research that could be used to develop biological weapons, according to the company's new AI misuse report that was obtained by The New York Times.

The report said Anthropic was unable to determine if the research 'served a legitimate or nefarious purpose'.

The firm said valid biological inquiry can result in scientific breakthroughs like vaccines, but the company erred on the side of caution because that same research could also be used to create dangerous pathogens.

Scientists involved in the incident allegedly circumvented controls preventing users from 'blocked regions' accessing its AI models.

The company claims the researchers, whose accounts have since been banned, worked to 'obfuscate the purpose of their research to evade our safeguards.'

The names of the researchers or institutions it had blocked were not disclosed by Anthropic, nor the countries in which these scientists are from.

The report also omitted which specific biological agents were at issue, with the company arguing this was because it is unclear what the aim of the research was.

The report, which was published Thursday, detailed several misuses of Anthropic's AI models - including chatbot Claude - over the past eight months.

In one example, a scientist asked Claude for assistance in writing a grant application for funding to conduct experimental research on the chikungunya virus.

Chikungunya virus is a mosquito-borne illness that causes a sudden high fever, severe debilitating pain, and other symptoms.

A vaccine for the chikungunya virus is already in existence, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

Anthropic notes research on the virus could be legitimately used in vaccine development, but also could result in manufacturing a superbug version of the disease.

The company claims it found this case particularly worrisome because the work was going to be performed at a military research institute.

Jacob Klein, the head of threat intelligence at Anthropic, told The New York Times: 'What we don't know is if the research was meant to be weaponised. But a military institution doing gain-of-function research is concerning.

'The fact that Russia, China and North Korea continue to develop prohibited biological weapons makes it imperative that we deny their researchers access to these extraordinarily capable models,' added Andrew Weber, a senior fellow on the Council on Strategic Risks.

Weber, who reviewed Anthropic's report before its release, said the findings were 'chilling examples of state-sponsored biological weapons developers tapping into the rapidly advancing capabilities' of AI.

The report also found China, Russia and Yemen attempted to use Claude to develop software to design firearms, missiles, armed drones and bombs.

Suspected Chinese and Iranian government-actors were found to have been targeting dissident and diaspora communities for surveillance, according to the report.

Russian state media was also found to be using Claude to generate election propaganda, including fabricated claims about the parliamentary election in Moldova.

Anthropic were approached by the Daily Mail for comment.
news.summary: A proposal brought to Parliament posited the creation of a legal mechanism allowing Britain to deactivate an AI model in the event of an emergency.

news.title: Trending World
news.text:
By: Emmanuel Kusi

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s visit to Canada comes as Kyiv and its allies seek to strengthen Ukraine’s defences and continue diplomatic efforts.

For Ukrainians, the war has brought separation, loss and uncertainty. Families have been torn apart, children displaced, civilians detained and communities damaged. Behind the statistics are people waiting for loved ones and hoping to return to normal life.

Zelenskyy’s September 9–11 visit includes discussions on defence, energy and economic cooperation. In Calgary on Thursday, he said air defence and winter preparations were priorities, as Russian attacks continue to threaten Ukraine’s infrastructure and civilians.

The diplomatic effort extends beyond Canada. U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner recently held talks in Moscow and Kyiv to discuss ways to end the war. Zelenskyy described some proposals as constructive, but the meetings produced no breakthrough. U.S. President Donald Trump has since said that Russian President Vladimir Putin expressed a willingness to make a deal. However, officials in Ukraine, the United States and Europe remain sceptical of Moscow’s intentions.

Europe remains central to Ukraine’s future. On Thursday, NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte said that Russia’s continued aggression is strengthening European resolve to bolster defence capabilities and support Kyiv. Canada and the European Union have also reaffirmed their cooperation on security and on support for Ukraine’s sovereignty and territorial integrity.

For Canadians, Zelenskyy’s visit raises a broader question: what role should Canada play in a war thousands of kilometres away?

Ottawa’s involvement extends beyond military assistance. Canada says its partnership with Ukraine covers defence, recovery, reconstruction, energy and economic cooperation, and support for a just and lasting peace.

Any settlement will also need to address civilian protection, separated families, and people who have been detained or displaced.

Zelenskyy’s visit is part of a broader debate about what ending the war should entail for Ukraine and for those who have endured it.

For Ukraine, the real test of any peace deal will be whether families are reunited, communities restored, and people can live without fear.

The 92-year-old former leader, who was prime minister at the time of the attacks, drew a standing ovation after telling his “American friends” that Canadians may be tolerant and kind but “we bow to no one”. US Ambassador to Canada Pete Hoekstra rose afterwards and hugged him.
“I say that not in anger, but as one friend to another,” Chretien said. “Friends need to be honest with each other.”
The unusually blunt remarks came during a solemn ceremony honouring the nearly 3,000 people killed in New York, at the Pentagon and aboard Flight 93, and remembering Gander’s extraordinary response to the attacks.
Gander, Newfoundland, opened its arms to nearly 6,600 airline passengers diverted there when the US government shut down airspace during September 11.

The remarks came at a striking moment in Canada-US relations. The long-time allies are embroiled in a trade war under US President Donald Trump, who has repeatedly talked about making Canada the 51st US state.
Chretien recalled how Canada rallied behind the US after the attacks, when Americans were “our neighbours, our closest friends under attack”.
“It was a day when we saw the worst of humanity and the very best,” he said. Some of the very best, he said, happened in Gander.
On September 11, 2001, 38 planes carrying more than 6,500 passengers and crew were diverted to the small Newfoundland town after the US shut its airspace. The arrivals nearly doubled Gander’s population.
Residents in Gander and surrounding communities turned schools, churches and meeting halls into shelters, supplied food and medicine and welcomed strangers into their homes. The stranded travellers became known locally as the “plane people”.
American passenger Raphael Fusco, who was 17 when his flight from Milan to Newark was diverted to Newfoundland, said Gander left him with a different memory of September 11.
“So while the rest of the world was seeing these horrific images, we saw something very different,” he said. “We saw extraordinary kindness.”
“They also opened their hearts,” Chretien said. “Because that is what I call the Canadian way. When our friends are in trouble, we don’t hesitate. We act.”

Hoekstra also received applause as he thanked Gander and Canada for standing with Americans then and in the years since. “Thank you to the people of Gander. Thank you for your friendship,” he said.
Hoekstra called those who responded 25 years ago “extraordinary people doing extraordinary things”.
“Beds? Check. Food? Check. Medicine? Check. Roof over their head? Check,” he said. “You stood up. You did what was needed to be done.”
His warm reception was notable because Hoekstra’s participation had itself generated controversy. Gander officials defended inviting him after criticism of his planned appearance, saying his attendance did not amount to an endorsement of the Trump administration.
“September 11 is bigger than politics, personalities or titles,” the town said.
The story of what happened in Gander inspired the hit Broadway musical Come From Away, and passengers and residents have continued returning for reunions.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney had used a campaign stop in Gander last year to say his nation was mourning “a friendship lost” with the United States.
Canada-US trade negotiations collapsed last month after Carney rejected proposed terms he said threatened Canadian sovereignty and key industries.
Washington imposed steep new tariffs, Canada retaliated this week and the Trump administration responded with additional restrictions on Canadian goods and access to US government contracts.

Against that backdrop, Chretien said Canada’s willingness to help should not be misread.
“Never mistake our tolerance for lack of determination,” he said. “And never, never mistake our kindness for softness.”
“Building a country like this, with this climate and this geography, is a sign of toughness, not of weakness,” Chretien said.
He recalled Canadians and Americans fighting together in Afghanistan after the attacks and the long history of the countries standing beside one another. Chretien noted that 165 Canadians died in Afghanistan, including 158 members of the Canadian Armed Forces.
“We embrace our friends and we help them in their moment of need, but we bow to no one,” Chretien said. “And the more we are insulted, threatened and abused, the more we will stand up for ourselves and stand united.”
Hoekstra, whose parents were liberated in the Netherlands by Allied forces that included Canadians during World War II, also invoked the countries’ history of shared sacrifice.
“We stood side by side,” he said.
Chretien ended not by rejecting that friendship but by calling for its restoration on terms Canada could accept.
“Respect, friendship and good neighbours,” he said. “Long live the United States and long live Canada.”

WITH AIR FORCE One expected to touch down at Dublin Airport early today, Ireland is bracing itself for the arrival of US President Donald Trump and one of the biggest security operations in the history of the State. 

Trump is expected to travel with an entourage of 1,000 people, including secret service agents.

On the Irish side, a 3,000-strong security team made up of gardaí and Defence Forces members be involved in the 48-hour operation.

Declared an “extraordinary event” by Garda Commissioner Justin Kelly, garda leave will be curtailed for the weekend, and members of the force will be expected to work overtime. 

The visit is expected to cost the Irish State in the region of €20 million.

The US President’s two days in Ireland for the Amgen Irish Open, hosted at his hotel in Doonbeg, will bring significant disruption to Dublin and Clare. 

Trump will spend the majority of his time at his Trump International Golf Links & Hotel in Doonbeg, which he purchased in 2014. 

The Journal / YouTube

But before the US President gets stuck into the golf, he will get the political engagements out of the way early in the day. 

Advertisement

Tánaiste Simon Harris is expected to meet Trump on the tarmac at Dublin Airport as he disembarks from Air Force One at around 8am. 

Trump will then travel by motorcade to the Phoenix Park, where he will pay a visit to President Catherine Connolly at the Áras.

Be warned, there will be significant road closures around Dublin from 7.30am until approximately 9.30am, with the M50 shut for rolling intervals to facilitate security escorts for the US president.

Also, if you were hoping to go to Dublin Zoo or for a run around the Phoenix Park at any point today, you may change your plans as the entire area will be shut down until after 6pm – possibly earlier, depending on how the timings of the day go.

In general, Dublin Airport has advised passengers to allow extra time for travel on Saturday. It said the airport will operate as normal, but passengers may have to take alternative routes to access the airport. 

Trump’s visit with Connolly will be short and probably more formal than sweet (remember, Connolly protested Trump’s visit to Ireland in 2019 when she was a TD). It is expected to last no more than 30 minutes in total, with 10 minutes of this being a closed meeting.

Connolly’s office declined to say what would be on the agenda for the meeting, with an update instead due after it takes place.

At around 10am, Trump will depart the Áras for Farmleigh, where he will have a short bilateral meeting with Taoiseach Micheál Martin.

After this, he will visit the US Ambassador’s residence in the Phoenix Park at approximately 11am, where he will address a private gathering of hundreds of guests. The guest list for the gathering has remained under wraps, but a number of Irish ministers are expected to attend.

Following the get-together in the ambassador’s residence, it is back to Dublin Airport at around 1pm for Trump, who will then fly to Shannon Airport before making his way by Marine One helicopter to Trump International Golf Links & Hotel.

Again, there will be major disruption to traffic around Dublin at this time, with the M50 closed at intervals between midday and 1pm approximately to facilitate Trump’s movements.

Once Trump arrives at his hotel for the Irish Open, it is very much seen as an “informal” day for the US President, a known golf lover.

And just like in Dublin, expect significant traffic delays in West Clare on Saturday afternoon.

Trump will then spend the night in his five-star resort and is expected to present the winner with their trophy alongside Taoiseach Micheál Martin on Sunday evening before departing Ireland later that night. 

First Lady Melania Trump, who attended a 9/11 memorial event with Trump on Friday, is not expected to travel, but his sons Donald Jnr and Eric will be taking part in the visit.

Niall Kelly / The 42 / The 42

A number of protests, supported by opposition parties Sinn Féin, Labour, Social Democrats, the Greens and People Before Profit, will take place in both Dublin and Clare over the weekend.

You can stay up to date with the visit today by following along with The Journal’s liveblog.

We’ll also have reporters covering events in the Phoenix Park and at Doonbeg, and the planned protests in Dublin city centre.

news.title: US President Donald Trump set to touch down in Ireland
news.text:
US President Donald Trump is due to land in Ireland this morning.

He will touch down on Saturday morning amid what has been described as one of the biggest security operations ever implemented by the Irish police service (An Garda Síochána).

Mr Trump will take part in engagements in the Irish capital Dublin as well as at his golf resort in Doonbeg, Co Clare, which is hosting the Irish Open.

Irish premier Micheál Martin said he looks forward to welcoming Mr Trump to Ireland and “discussing the many issues of mutual interest and reaffirming the strong economic, cultural and people-to-people ties between Ireland and the United States”.

“His visit comes during a remarkable sporting summer for Ireland, and the United States and this weekend’s Irish Open at Trump International Doonbeg will be a fitting conclusion to an outstanding season of sport, and I hope we will see an Irish winner lifting the trophy on Sunday,” he added.

He is expected to meet President Catherine Connolly, a long-standing critic of the US president, at her official residence Áras an Uachtaráin in Dublin’s Phoenix Park, before a nearby engagement with Mr Martin, the Taoiseach at the Farmleigh Estate.

He will also attend a series of events at Deerfield, the residence of the US Ambassador to Ireland.

A number of protests against Mr Trump’s visit have been planned.

Garda Commissioner Justin Kelly said peaceful protest would be facilitated as much as possible, but there will be “no tolerance” for public disorder or attempts to impact “critical movements” of the US president.

“We have robust policing plans in place and will arrest and prosecute those committing offences”, he said, adding that water cannon will be “on standby” but said he hoped they would not be needed.

Ireland’s deputy premier Simon Harris will welcome Mr Trump as he arrives off Air Force One at Dublin Airport early on Saturday morning.

Speaking ahead of the moment, the Tánaiste said the visit offers an “opportunity to mark and reflect on the deep and enduring links between Ireland and the United States”.

“I am looking forward to getting a chance to meet again with President Trump following a brief engagement on the margins of the UN General Assembly in New York last year,” he said.

“Ireland and the US have deep and enduring political, economic, cultural and historical links that transcend the administrations on both sides of the Atlantic.

“There are clear benefits from high-level visits such as this as they offer an opportunity to engage on the deep economic relationship between our two countries which creates prosperity, jobs and opportunity for large numbers of people here and in the US.”

Mr Harris said Mr Trump’s visit will be an opportunity for the Irish Government to engage substantively as the US remains Ireland’s largest trading and investment partner.

“More than 900 US companies directly employ 245,000 people in Ireland, while more than 200,000 people are directly employed by almost 800 Irish companies in the US,” he said.

“Our economic partnership delivers for both countries. US firms present in Ireland have contributed to an economic ecosystem that has driven improvements in productivity and encouraged Irish companies to scale and grow in the US and internationally.”

The visit will cause significant disruption and road closures around Dublin Airport and across the capital city as well as in Co Clare and Shannon Airport which will also be used by Mr Trump.
news.summary: Mr Trump is expected to visit the Irish capital Dublin as well as his golf course in Doonbeg, Co Clare.
news.author: Rebecca Black

news.title: Donald Trump 'appears to fall asleep' at 9/11 Pentagon memorial sparking outrage
news.text: US President Donald Trump has provoked criticism online after footage from one of the services marking the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 attacks appeared to show him dozing off. He was present at a ceremony at the Pentagon, honouring the lives lost when al Qaida militants hijacked aircraft and killed nearly 3,000 people across three locations. Trump had opted to attend this event instead of joining all previous living presidents at the memorial at the former World Trade Center site in New York . Viewers spotted the 80 year old appearing to have drifted off in his seat during proceedings, which were broadcast extensively across news networks. Images and footage from the occasion show first lady Melania Trump looking stony-faced as her husband nods off. At one point, his head tilted back and his mouth hung open. Furious viewers flocked to social media to condemn him for showing disrespect to the victims of the attack, reports the Express . Writing on X, one user posted: " Joe Biden , 83 years-old, battling Stage 4 cancer that's spread to his bones, stood for hours alongside Dr. Jill Biden, as the names of the 9/11 victims were read. Donald Trump fell asleep at the 9/11 Memorial at the Pentagon. One showed respect while Trump was an embarrassment." Another commented: "Trump disrespected 2,977 people murdered on 9/11 by not attending the NY memorial service...Then he falls asleep at the Pentagon service. He doesn't care about anyone but himself." A third chimed in: "Trump fell asleep at the Pentagon during the ceremony for 9/11. He has fallen asleep during a cage fight, a basketball game, July 4th fireworks, and multiple times in the Oval Office with people talking directly to him. There is something seriously wrong with him." A fourth raged: "Trump sleeping at this 9-11 memorial is SO OFFENSIVE TO ALL AMERICANS! ! !". A fifth fumed: "It's disgusting that trump not only refused to attend the 9/11 memorial in NYC...but he was so disinterested at the Pentagon ceremony that he fell asleep. Meanwhile a sixth raged: "You're a disgrace Trump falling to sleep at pentagon ceremony. "". The US president has faced mounting criticism since his return to the White House, following a string of public blunders and what appear to be visible bruising and swelling. The Republican leader has reportedly been caught dozing off in public on numerous occasions over the past 12 months, with many of these incidents occurring during official engagements. Among the notable appearances at which he has allegedly been spotted nodding off are the Pennsylvania Energy and Innovation Summit, the Antifa roundtable, an obesity-drug press conference, the signing of the Whole Milk for Healthy Kids Act, and Pope Francis' funeral.
news.summary: Donald Trump was attending a ceremony at the Pentagon, commemorating the lives lost when al Qaida militants hijacked planes and killed nearly 3,000 people in three locations

news.title: Donald Trump lashes out at ABC News reporter Rachel Scott during tense exchange on Dallas airport tarmac
news.text:
US President Donald Trump has lashed out at an ABC News reporter on a Texas airport tarmac, repeatedly shutting down her questions as he prepared to leave Dallas.

The tense exchange unfolded on Thursday, September 10, as ABC News senior political correspondent Rachel Scott attempted to question Mr Trump about his pledge to give every American adult $US5000 if Republicans win the midterm elections.

“Not you, not you. Hey, not you,” Mr Trump, 80, said, wagging his finger at Scott, 33.

Mr Trump emphasised his final “not you” by stepping towards the journalist and leaning down in her direction before turning to take questions from other reporters.

ABC News has since publicly backed Scott following the confrontation.

“We wholeheartedly support Rachel Scott and our entire Washington team who do an exceptional job delivering trusted and straightforward reporting to the public every single day,” an ABC News spokesperson said in a statement.

Scott has not publicly addressed the incident beyond posting footage of the exchange on X alongside the caption, “My question to Trump tonight.”

It is far from the first heated exchange between Mr Trump and Scott, with the President repeatedly taking aim at the journalist and her reporting since returning to the White House.

During an appearance at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool in May, Mr Trump turned towards a group of construction workers before describing Scott as “stupid,” “one of the worst reporters” and “a horror show.”

The President also declared her questions were “a disgrace to our country” after she questioned him about his focus on projects in Washington DC while the US was at war with Iran and Americans faced rising petrol prices.

The White House later shared footage of that exchange on X with the caption, “@POTUS destroys ABC Fake News reporter.”

Another fiery encounter unfolded during a White House Cabinet meeting in December 2025, when Scott questioned Mr Trump over US airstrikes on boats off the coast of Venezuela that his administration accused of carrying drugs.

“You are the most obnoxious reporter in the whole place,” Trump said when Scott asked if he would commit to releasing the full video of a recent strike that triggered allegations it could qualify as a war crime. “Let me just tell you, you are an obnoxious — a terrible reporter.”

Separate analyses by The New York Times and London-based nonprofit Airwars found US strikes in the region had killed at least 227 people during the past 12 months, none of whom had been formally charged with a crime.

The pair’s history of tense exchanges stretches back to Mr Trump’s 2024 presidential campaign.

During an appearance at the National Association of Black Journalists convention, Scott asked Mr Trump “why should Black voters trust you”.

“I don’t think I’ve ever been asked a question in such a horrible manner,” he responded.

“I think it’s disgraceful that I came here in good spirit. I love the Black population of this country, I’ve done so much for the Black population of this country,” he replied.

Later during the July 2024 interview, Mr Trump questioned whether then-Vice President Kamala Harris was really Black.

Mr Trump’s clashes with female journalists have also extended beyond Scott, with the White House forced to defend his language towards reporters in November 2025.

That month, the President described New York Times reporter Katie Rogers as “ugly, both inside and out” and snapped, “Quiet. Quiet, Piggy” at Bloomberg correspondent Catherine Lucey aboard Air Force One.

“Look, the president is very frank and honest with everyone in this room,” then-White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt said in defense of Trump’s “piggy” remark. “I think everyone in this room should appreciate the frankness and the openness that you get from President Trump on a near-daily basis.”

Mr Trump has also repeatedly clashed with CNN’s Kaitlan Collins and New York Times reporter Maggie Haberman.

The President has taken to calling Haberman “Maggot” and on Tuesday, September 8, described her as “unattractive, both inside and out”.

The New York Times hit back the following day, accusing the President of attacking journalists over reporting he does not like.

“This is another all too common example of the president lashing out at coverage he doesn’t like and belittling journalists who report the facts,” the Times said in a statement on Wednesday, Sept. 9.
news.summary: US President Donald Trump has been caught in a tense confrontation with a female reporter after lunging towards her and shutting down her question.
news.author: Madeline Cove

A crypto-billionaire has made a record £36million donation to Reform.

Ben Delo, the co-founder of a crypto trading platform, said he wants Nigel Farage’s party to have a ‘fair fight’ at the next general election.

Mr Delo was already Reform’s second-largest donor and said he made the new gift following a difficult summer for Reform, as he believes ‘they should spend less time trying to raise funds’ and concentrate on preparing for government.

Mr Farage’s party is currently under investigation by Scotland Yard over separate claims it has breached donation law.

Last week, a Channel 4 undercover sting alleged that two senior members of Mr Farage’s team had sought to circumvent the rules on foreign donations.

Reform denies any wrongdoing.

The previous record donation of £10million was bequeathed to the Conservatives. Mr Delo had given Reform £8m in the past, behind only a £9m donation by fellow crypto-king Christopher Harborne.

A £5m gift from Thai-based Mr Harborne to Mr Farage is the subject of a parliamentary sleaze inquiry.

The Reform leader initially said it was to pay for security for the rest of his life before later suggesting it was a ‘reward’ for his years of Brexit campaigning.

He called his summer’s farcical Clacton by-election in a bid to draw a line under the scrutiny. But the investigation restarted after he retained the seat. All other major parties refused to take part in the ballot, leaving comedy candidate Count Binface as Mr Farage’s main challenger.

The record gift means Reform has now raised five times as much as the Conservatives and six times as much as Labour this year alone.

Mr Delo made his first billion just four years after founding his crypto firm, BitMex, in 2014.

He pleaded guilty to failing to implement an anti-money laundering programme in the US in 2022 but was pardoned by president Donald Trump last year.

‘Unlike the people who express mock concern for the health of “our democracy” while doing everything they can to keep it as a cartel, I want a fair fight and a level playing field,’ he told The Telegraph last night.

He pledged £36million to the party after vowing to give Reform £1million a month between now and the latest possible general election date in 2029.

But, he said, he would gift it in one go to defy any Government bid to block the donations.

It comes after Labour put a cap of £100,000 on donations political parties could receive from overseas donors.

Mr Delo, who recently moved back to the UK from Hong Kong as a result, took a swipe at the move, as well as further reform on party funding in Labour’s Representation of the People Bill.

He lambasted it as ‘an attempt at election rigging’, adding that Labour’s millions from unions would be unaffected.

Mr Farage said he was ‘honoured’ and ‘humbled’ by the gift.

The money, it is understood, will be used to allow Reform to recruit ‘the best brains’ to its policy unit and expand the number of campaign managers it has.

‘This is about preparing for government,’ said a senior party source, with Reform convinced Prime Minister Andy Burnham is set to call an early election.

A Labour Party spokesperson said: ‘Nigel Farage is still up to his neck in scandal over his secret £5 million “gift” from his other crypto-billionaire backer and the criminal investigation into potentially illegal donations. The questions he faces aren’t going away – in fact they’re piling up.

‘Reform UK can’t buy their way out of questions about sleaze, criminal mates and dodgy finances.

‘It’s time Farage and Reform finally came clean with the public, co-operated fully with the police, and proved they’re not just in it for themselves.
news.summary: Ben Delo, the co-founder of a crypto trading platform, made the donation following a difficult summer for Reform and wants the party to concentrate on preparing for government.

news.title: Trump biographer says sun-downing Trump is really hating his 'long goodbye'
news.text:
A journalist and author with multiple inside sources into President Donald Trump's White House says Trump is unquestioningly fading into the background — and he must be furious.

“It’s all about attention because A: he can’t resist the idea of it, and B: because the idea of someone else getting the attention is anathema to him,” said Trump biographer Michael Wolff, speaking to co-host Joanna Coles about Trump’s desperate bid to launch a “Trump-a-Palooza” in Dallas, as Wolff described it. 

“But I think there’s a longer-term strategy [behind the festival],” Wolff added. “Trump does not want the Republican Party to ever imagine life without him.”

“Remember we are going into this other phase,” Wolff explained. “In a president’s second term, after the midterms, the president begins the ‘long goodbye.’ His possible successors come to the forefront. Okay, that’s not going to happen here, and you can see this convention’s announcement of that. ‘I am not going away. I am going to play this in the total opposite of that.’”

In another "Inside Trump's Head" podcast episode, Wolff and co-host Joanna Coles had discussed the shadow of death Trump must feel creeping closer after the spate of recent celebrity deaths.

“Eighty is a seriously mortal moment,” said Wolff, who is best known for his extensive coverage of Trump's political career, including several books about his first term based on purported insider sources. “You’re in your 80s. This is your 9th decade.”

Wolff described Trump as a morbidly overweight octogenarian who is now also being faced with a recent slate of celebrity deaths, making him question his own mortality even harder.

“When I see people who are my age who go down, I register it. I think everybody does,” said Wolff. “Everybody does, but in particular a 300lb pound man who stuffs himself with poison and who hasn’t done a lick of exercise ever might have an even more immediate reaction to other people’s mortality at his age.”

But Trump’s reaction to his rapidly encroaching end appears to be to deny it at the top of his lungs.

“The cult of personality is going to go into hyperdrive now,” warned Wolff.

“Ugh,” Coles groaned. 

“He’s saying ‘I’m not going to allow the party, the country or the world to get me, Donald Trump, out of its head,’” Wolff continued, adding that Trump understands “that his talent is getting inside other people’s heads and staying there.”

Coles suggested a personality like Trump would even be offended with having to compete — even for a day — with the deaths of thousands of Americans on the 25th anniversary of 9-11.

“How is he going to react when the 9-11 event on Friday, because he’s a New Yorker, and he’s not going to be there,” said Coles. “The other presidents are going to be there, so George W. Bush, Barack Obama, Joe Biden, the Clintons will all be there, and he won’t be there. They’ve automatically upstaged his RNC-palooza.”

“Oh, he’s hoping his Trump-a-Palooza will upstage 9-11,” assured Wolff. “That’s what this whole Trump-a-palooza is all about. I’m sure he’s been stewing about that, saying ‘I should’ve been there. I should’ve gone down there. I should’ve gotten some pictures of me there [at the tower collapse].

“Exactly,” laughed Coles. “Where are the pictures? There would have been pictures had he been there, but there aren’t. There are just hilarious fake AI videos of firemen carting him out. … and tweets of him as a heroic figure, when people were literally jumping from the buildings.”

“It’s unspeakable. It’s unconscionable,” said Wolff. “But Trump sees this and he’s triangulating it. It’s not just happenstance. This whole idea of a mini convention. He demanded this. He ordered this into place [to upstage it].

news.title: Trump administration has no plans to strike Houthis for now, 2 US officials say
news.text:
The Trump administration is offering significant intelligence and targeting assistance to Saudi Arabia but does not currently plan on launching direct military attacks against the Houthis, two U.S. officials told ABC News. 

Both officials cautioned that the administration’s thinking could change, particularly if the threat to Red Sea shipping lanes escalates significantly.

As part of the U.S.' support for Saudi Arabia, U.S. Central Command commander Adm. Brad Cooper traveled to the country for meetings on Thursday, according to one of the officials. Central Command declined to comment.

Crown Prince Mohammad bin Salman spoke with President Donald Trump about the situation twice on Thursday, one official said, adding that the Saudi leader was seeking direct military intervention from the U.S. but that he did not indicate it was absolutely critical. 

"The United States is focused on protecting our core national security interests—such as ensuring freedom of navigation in the Red Sea -- while empowering our regional partners to take the lead in managing and resolving regional security challenges,” a senior Trump administration official said when asked about the president’s calls with bin Salman. "We are in continuous dialogue with Saudi Arabia and the Republic of Yemen Government regarding regional stability.” 

Another official said the Saudi government has communicated in recent days a willingness to launch a major military operation against the Houthis, even if it means going it alone, but that Riyadh had not yet made a final decision. 

Both officials said that the Trump administration is continuing to closely monitor the situation in Yemen and that although assessments from earlier Friday indicated that the Houthis had taken control of the country’s west coast, Yemeni government forces and aligned militias were continuing to fight back and the situation could still change rapidly without outside intervention. 

The Houthis and their Iranian backers are aware that attempting to choke off traffic in the Strait of Bab al-Mandeb would very likely trigger a stronger response from Saudi Arabia, the U.S., and potentially other countries. They have issued multiple statements indicating the strait is open to commercial traffic, but Houthi strikes on Saudi-linked ships have increased the risk level for all vessels, according to analysts.
news.summary: The U.S. is offering intel and targeting assistance to Saudi Arabia, they say.

 Phase one repairs 90 per cent complete at Holland Primary School 







MONTEGO BAY, Jamaica—Phase one rehabilitation at Holland Primary School in St Elizabeth is now 90 per cent complete, says State Minister in the Ministry of Education, Skills, Youth and Information Rhoda Moy Crawford.

Speaking to JIS News during a visit to the institution on Thursday, September 10, to get a firsthand look at the progress of the works, she said that the project is “progressing rapidly”.

The first segment is focused primarily on repairing hurricane damage, including completely re-roofing the main classroom block, bathrooms, and the principal’s office. The classrooms have also been fitted with ceiling fans.

Phase two works will address other longstanding needs at the school.

Crawford said that students are being accommodated in tents until the rehabilitation works are completed.

An additional tent will be provided, as well as the installation of temporary timber classrooms, which is expected to be completed by the end of the week.

Crawford said students have expressed satisfaction with the temporary arrangements, including the tents, which she noted are well ventilated.

“Some students in grade one, I believe, or grade two students, were just expressing to us how much they love the tents and how cool the tents are, and we’re assuring them that we are working hard to have their classrooms reconstructed and ready,” she told JIS News.

The state minister clarified that the school’s use of outdoor classes earlier this week was not due to a lack of temporary classroom space, noting that outdoor learning is part of an existing practice at the institution.

“The use of outdoor spaces for teaching and learning was not born out of a need; it was a choice. The teacher decided that she wanted to take the students out,” she told JIS News.

Principal of Holland Primary School, Simone Doctor, explained further that the school established an outdoor “reading nook” in March as part of a photo challenge to identify an area on the compound that could be rehabilitated and used for educational activities.

She said the space has since been used for teaching and learning and was utilised during the week.

“So, the students were very comfortable there, the teachers were very comfortable there, and teaching,” she noted.

“Our students are at school, they are happy, they are learning, and they look forward to coming to school every day,” she told JIS News.

Doctor expressed gratitude to the Ministry for its response to the school’s needs following Hurricane Melissa, noting that rehabilitation works began in January and are continuing.

“I’d like to commend the Ministry of Education, Skills, Youth, and Information for the response and the effort towards the reconstruction of our school,” she said.

Doctor also acknowledged the support of Region Five Education Officer, Collette Morris Plummer, who she said has been involved with the institution since the reopening of school and assisted with preparations.

news.title: De Niro calls controversial Mamdani police comments 'ridiculous' as he defends mayor going to 9/11 service
news.text: Outspoken liberal actor Robert De Niro agreed with some of Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s critics that his comments on law enforcement were "ridiculous," but still argued he should attend Friday’s 9/11 memorial. Political rancor has threatened to cast a long shadow over this year's Sept. 11 remembrance events, marking 25 years since the tragedy that rocked the United States. New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani's past rhetoric and links to terror sympathizers are spurring intense backlash ahead of the city's events memorializing the World Trade Center attacks, with Republicans and people whose lives were changed by the attacks demanding he not attend. The Hollywood Reporter noted the controversy when it spoke to De Niro in an interview published Thursday, asking, "Do you think he should be there?" "I don’t see why he shouldn’t come," De Niro said. "He’s the mayor. I haven’t heard him say or do anything yet that would disqualify him from being there. Maybe I’m naive, but you have to give the guy a chance. He’s not a part of what happened." MAMDANI HEADS TO 9/11 MEMORIAL DESPITE 110,000-SIGNATURE PUSH FROM VICTIMS’ FAMILIES TO STAY AWAY One of the past comments Mamdani has been grilled about repeatedly is his criticism of the NYPD amid the George Floyd riots of 2020. Mamdani called to "defund the police" in 2020 and labeled the NYPD "racist, anti-queer, and a major threat to public safety." When De Niro was asked further about whether he could understand why some families would find it problematic, he paused for a moment and answered, "I understand their pain, but I still think he should be there." "I think this stems from tension he’s had with the fire department and the comments about defund the police, which I don’t think he really meant," the interviewer added. "Well he did say it. And, of course, it’s ridiculous," De Niro said. "You can’t defund the police. It’s not going to happen. But I still think he should be at the memorial." He went on to suggest Mamdani could use the opportunity "as a bridge" to unite people. When asked about President Donald Trump, however, De Niro offered a far sharper reply, saying, "We have to stop him. It’s insane. We have to send people to voting booths and make sure they can go in. Just watch to keep them safe. It’s crazy we’re here, but this is where we are. We have to protect our elections." Entertainment commentator Christian Toto responded to the actor’s interview. "The Hollywood Reporter eggs on Robert De Niro, sans fact checking, because it agrees with most of what he says. The outlet understands the actor's lack of information on key political subjects, too, but it cheers him on because he's anti-Trump and anti-GOP," Toto told Fox News Digital. "Meanwhile, the actor hasn't a clue about the mayor's past comments, his toxic associations or why his 'defund the police' beliefs are so damaging. He's a Useful Idiot for the Left, and The Hollywood Reporter is all too happy to magnify his idiocy," he added. 9/11 FAMILIES PUSH TO BAN MAMDANI FROM 25TH ANNIVERSARY REMEMBRANCE OVER 'HOSTILE' RECORD An online petition led by family members of people killed on Sept. 11 — signed by over 100,000 people — has called on Mamdani to skip the memorial. "Mr. Mamdani has praised Brooklyn Imam Siraj Wahhaj, who has been linked to radical Islam, was named as an alleged co-conspirator in the 1993 World Trade Center bombing, and served as a character witness for the 'Blind Sheikh,' who was convicted in 1995 of plotting terror attacks against the United States," the petition said. "Mr. Mamdani has endorsed candidates such as Aber Kawas, who described 9/11 as an attack 'a couple of people did in the context of U.S. capitalism, racism, White supremacy, and Islamophobia,' and who also expressed sympathy for Ahmed Ferhani, who pleaded guilty to plotting to blow up a Manhattan synagogue," it added. Mamdani and other socialist candidates' association with far-left activist Hasan Piker has also gotten intense scrutiny over Piker's past comments that the United States "deserved" the attacks, remarks he promptly walked back at the time but continue to haunt him and his political circle. Mamdani has also condemned the comment. Mamdani has faced backlash for giving a ceremonial pen from a 9/11 remembrance ceremony to a top aide who once represented a convicted al Qaeda member. Mamdani had handed the pen to his chief counsel, Ramzi Kassem. Kassem previously represented Ahmed al-Darbi, who pleaded guilty to war crime charges tied to al Qaeda plots against commercial ships and was the brother-in-law of Khalid al-Mihdhar, one of the hijackers aboard American Airlines Flight 77, which crashed into the Pentagon, killing 184. Rafael Mangual, the head of research for the Manhattan Institute’s Policing & Public Safety Initiative, argued that De Niro and the interviewer sorely missed the mark in recalling Mamdani's record. "I’m not sure I share Mr. DeNiro’s dismissal of calls for Mayor Mamdani to keep away from the official memorial ceremony at the site of the World Trade Center on Friday," he said. "Nor do I think the mayor’s past expressions of vitriol for the NYPD — whose members bravely ran to the assistance of their fellow Americans that tragic morning 25 years ago — are the only justifications for the anger of the families that have expressed their preference for the mayor not to attend Friday’s ceremony." "As a rapper, Mamdani praised the Holy Land Five — a group convicted of providing material support to Hamas, an Islamist terrorist organization," Mangual continued. "On the mayoral campaign trail, Mamdani posed for a photo op with Siraj Wahaj, an unindicted co-conspirator in the 1993 World Trade Center bombing who also testified as a character witness on behalf of Sheik Omar Abdel-Rahman, who had lectured at Wahaj’s mosque prior to being convicted of several terrorism charges in the mid-1990s." "During his campaign, he also palled around with Hasan Piker, who stated that America deserved 9/11 and praised the mujahideen for shooting and wounding then-Navy SEAL and current Congressman Dan Crenshaw," he added. "And as mayor, Mamdani hired as his chief legal counsel Ramzi Kassem, who volunteered to represent pro bono a Guantanamo Bay detainee and convicted al-Qaeda terrorist Ahmed al-Darbi. When coupled with his vitriolic criticisms of the very institutions tasked with keeping us safe from terrorist threats, the wishes of the families De Niro was asked about become much harder to ignore." CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE Mary Marslender, a former Trump appointee and senior advisor to the U.S. Senate and now a Republican consultant, argued that Mamdani cannot outrun his past call to defund the police so easily. "Mamdani has spent years portraying New York’s brave first responders as the problem, and Robert De Niro knows that. Mamdani ran for mayor on a platform of defunding the police, only walking back his stance for political gain — not out of genuine conviction," she said. "He has also refused to distance himself from extremist voices who blame America for 9/11 and declined to condemn the phrase 'globalize the intifada,' claiming he won’t police language," Marslender added. "Robert De Niro’s defense of Mamdani’s views reflects a troubling disregard for the values that unite Americans." Former RNC National Spokesperson Elizabeth Pipko argued that De Niro has a long pattern of clumsy political commentary. "Robert De Niro is again showing his privilege and ignorance," she said. "He has decided because he aligns politically with Mamdani, he will defend him without knowing the facts. Similarly, he will attack Trump, even when discussing 9/11, because he dislikes him, again without knowing any facts." "Mamdani has said horrific things about the NYPD and those who protect our great country. Yes, but unfortunately, he has also praised a man that was named by federal prosecutors as a co-conspirator in connection with the 1993 World Trade Center bombing case," Marslender continued. "He campaigns with Hasan Piker, who has a framed photo of the Twin Towers burning standing on his desk. He refuses to condemn the phrase 'globalize the intifada.' Ironically, that phrase is exactly what 9/11 was about." "Just once, I’d like to see De Niro confronted with these facts and the sad reality of his own ignorance," she said. "I’d be curious what his excuses would be then." Fox News Digital reached out to Mamdani’s office for comment but did not immediately receive a response. PORTLAND, Jamaica — Newly-crowned Miss Universe Jamaica Celene Hall has arrived in her native Portland for a homecoming parade in her honour on Friday, two weeks after becoming the first woman from the parish to win the pageant.

The 25-year-old businesswoman beat 32 other contestants at the Grand Coronation in Kingston to become Jamaica’s latest beauty queen.

The event will culminate on Friday afternoon with a grand civic celebration at the Errol Flynn Marina in Port Antonio.
